activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by delaying ovulation, and they are more effective the sooner they are taken after unprotected sex.
story:
Grandma's porch smelled like lemon polish and the mint she grew in a coffee can, and that was where Carter sat on the first evening of spring break with a folder from Mr. Castillo balanced on his knees. Mr. Castillo had talked him into the peer health program with a single sentence: "You're the only sophomore who asked a follow-up question." The folder had sections on consent, on contraception, on where the clinic was and what a test involved, and Carter had promised to study it over break, mostly to avoid studying anything else.

Rodney arrived on a bike with a milk crate zip-tied to the rack, and he did not sit down. "Okay, don't be weird about it," he said. "Friday. Me and, let's say a person. The condom broke, and she's freaking out, and I'm freaking out on her behalf, and Emrik said you're doing the health thing now, so." He made a gesture that took in the whole folder. "Utilitarianism or whatever."

"That is not what this is." Carter was already flipping pages. "How long ago?"

"Like two days. Maybe a little more."

"Two days." Carter read faster. The pharmacy section had a fact boxed in highlighter, some note from a kid who'd taken the training last year, and the box said the pills mainly worked by delaying ovulation, and that they worked better the sooner they were taken. He looked up. "We're going now. Tonight. Waiting even a few more days is a real mistake, and I'm not expatiating on why, I'm telling you what the page says and we're moving."

Grandma intercepted them in the kitchen, where she was conducting experiments involving rhubarb. She raised one eyebrow at Rodney's milk crate as though it were a congenital condition. "Back by nine," she said, "and take the reflective vests, unless you'd prefer I drive behind you with the hazards on."

They pedaled to the pharmacy three streets over, where a pharmacist with reading glasses chained to her neck listened to Rodney's monologue and said, kindly, "You want the emergency contraceptive pill. It mainly delays ovulation, so it doesn't end anything that's already happened, it postpones it. And the sooner she takes it, the better it works, so tonight is a good plan." She rang it up, said it was fine to take it a couple of days after, just not as good as sooner, and slid a pamphlet across the counter like she was dealing cards.

Outside, in the glow of the vending machine, Rodney read the pamphlet twice. "I thought it was some kind of abort thing," he said. "That's why she was scared. She thought it was that."

"So you should tell her exactly what the pharmacist said. Delaying ovulation, better sooner." Carter was quiet for a second, because there was a question in the folder about this exact thing, about whether you explain to spare someone or explain to show off. "Also, and I'm saying this as your friend who has a folder, did she actually want to, Friday? Not just agreed to. Wanted to."

Rodney looked at the pamphlet instead of at him. "Yeah. She did. We talked about it before, and during." He said it like a kid who had done the reading and was relieved to be quizzed. "I keep thinking about the part where you can get tested even if nothing's wrong. Like a checkup."

"You can. There's a walk-in clinic two blocks from school, Mr. Castillo has the hours in here, and it's free if you're under eighteen." Carter tapped the folder. "You don't have to decide tonight. But you could go Tuesday, and it would be boring, which is the best thing a clinic can be."

They rode back under the streetlights, vests on, Rodney's milk crate rattling like a tambourine. Grandma was on the porch with tea for three, which was her way of asking without asking. Rodney drank his, called his person, and stood by the railing repeating, word for word, "mainly by delaying ovulation, and sooner is better," until he had it cold.

Carter sat with his cooling tea and thought that he still didn't know whether the folder made him wise or just early. He knew the pharmacy closed at nine, and that Rodney had ridden fast, and that somewhere a phone was ringing and being answered.

Grandma took the empty cups inside and called back through the screen door, "Tell Mr. Castillo the rhubarb will be ready in June."

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Economists count the wages a student gives up while studying full-time as part of the cost of college, along with tuition.
story:
Robert had spread the two envelopes on his bed like evidence in a trial he was conducting against himself. One held the acceptance letter from the state university, tuition figure circled twice in blue ink. The other held the offer from Kessler Electric, a two-year apprenticeship starting in July, with a wage printed in plain black type at the bottom of the page. He had read both so many times that the paper had gone soft at the folds, and the numbers had started to feel less like facts and more like opponents.

The room smelled of the sandwich his mother had left on the desk an hour ago, untouched, the cheese sweating under its plastic wrap. Through the wall he could hear his younger sister practicing her elocution exercises for the debate team, the same four sentences over and over, each repetition sharper than the last. He envied her, in a way. Her choice was only about whether to enter the tournament. His seemed to be about everything at once.

Henri arrived first, letting himself in through the back door the way he always did, and Jeremiah came ten minutes behind him with a bag of gas station licorice that he dropped on the bed between the envelopes. "Okay," Jeremiah said, sitting on the floor with his back against the mattress frame. "Show us the crime scene."

Robert walked them through it, slowly, the way he had walked himself through it at two in the morning. Tuition was one cost, but it wasn't the whole cost, and that was the part that had been eating at him since the open house. He'd been standing near a table where a girl about his age was asking a financial aid officer questions, and he'd overheard enough to stop him cold. She had been holding a calculator, comparing the tuition on the brochure with the paycheck she could earn if she skipped college and worked instead, and the officer had told her that economists counted those wages, the ones a student gives up while studying full-time, as part of the cost of college, right alongside tuition. Robert had repeated it to himself all the way to the parking lot, and then for a week afterward.

"So the real price," Henri said, turning the university letter over as though a smaller number might be hiding on the back, "is tuition plus everything Kessler would have paid you for four years."

"Two years of apprenticeship wages, then whatever comes after," Robert said. "Which is the part I can't calculate, because I don't know what comes after. That's the whole problem. The thing I'm giving up is a number I can't read yet."

Jeremiah tore off a piece of licorice and pointed the ragged end at him. "My cousin did this exact thing," he said. "Not school versus work, but he had to requisition the good truck from his dad's shop for a whole summer, and his dad said fine, but then he couldn't take the landscaping contract, because the truck can only be in one place. He still talks about the contract. He never talks about the truck."

"The truck didn't cost him anything," Henri said.

"The truck cost him the contract," Jeremiah said. "That's the point."

They argued about it for a while, the three of them, in the loose way they argued about everything, sprawled across the bed and the floor while the light through the blinds crept up the wall and dimmed. Henri thought the whole framing was cynical, a way of making every choice feel like a loss. Jeremiah thought refusing to do the math was worse, a kind of borrowed sentimentality, and he said so with his mouth full. Robert mostly listened, turning the Kessler letter over in his hands, and found himself thinking of Ms. Nguyen, who lived two houses down and who had retired from teaching economics at the community college. He'd been avoiding her for a week because he was afraid she'd hand him an answer, and he didn't want an answer. He wanted someone to tell him he was allowed to sit in the not-knowing.

He left his friends with the sandwich and the licorice and walked down the street in the flat gray evening. Ms. Nguyen was watering a pot of basil that had no business being alive this late in the season. "Robert," she said, without looking up. "You've been walking past my house very loudly for six days."

He told her everything, faster than he meant to, the letters and the wages and the girl with the calculator and the two friends with their two arguments. She let the soil soak before she spoke. "You're the only one who thinks both of them are partly right," she said. "That's not indecision, that's a position. You can hold it and still decide. Deciding doesn't mean pretending the other thing was worth nothing." She pinched off a sprig of basil and handed it to him. "What would the smallest version of the choice look like?"

Walking home, he worked it out. Kessler's apprentice class started in July; the university's fall term started in late August. There was a summer session at the community college, two courses, transferable, cheap, evenings. He could take the apprenticeship and the courses both, for one term, and find out which one actually felt like his life before he traded either one away entirely. It wasn't a solution so much as a narrowing of the question, and something loosened in his chest as he thought of it, like a hand unclenching.

Back in his bedroom, Henri and Jeremiah had fallen asleep in the wreck of his bed, the envelopes still pinned under Jeremiah's elbow. Robert sat down at his desk, pulled a fresh sheet of paper toward him, and wrote the two courses at the top. Then he peeled the plastic off the sandwich and, for the first time all day, ate the whole thing.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Supporters of lowering the US voting age to 18 used the slogan "old enough to fight, old enough to vote," because 18-year-olds could be drafted for the Vietnam War.
story:
Laurie had the ballot open in one browser tab and her grandmother's recipe for lemon bars open in another, and she kept switching between them as though the two decisions carried equal weight. The kitchen laptop sat where it always sat, on the counter beside the fruit bowl, and her father was pretending to unload the dishwasher without watching her, which meant he dropped a fork twice.

"It's not a test," he said. "Nobody grades it."

"That's exactly the problem," Laurie said. "If it were a test, there'd be a right answer." She had spent the previous evening in an archipelago of tabs, each one an island of someone insisting they alone were reasonable, and she had gone to bed with her ears ringing from opinions. This morning she'd started over with the actual voter guide, which was duller and better, like plain oatmeal after a week of candy.

She heard herself say it and paused. Somewhere in the last month she had begun to internalize the idea that a choice made calmly was worth more than one made loudly, though she couldn't have said when that started.

Down the hall, her grandfather was on the phone with his sister, arguing about the school board race the way they argued about everything, which was with total commitment and zero malice. His voice carried. Laurie's father winced at the volume and mouthed sorry, and Laurie waved it off, because honestly the shouting was comforting, like weather.

She got stuck on the county measure about the water district. Caden had texted her a long message calling the whole thing a scam, and Margot had texted a longer one calling Caden doctrinaire, which he was, though Margot could be too, and Laurie had replied to both with the thumbs-up that means I am not doing this tonight. She read the measure again. It was four paragraphs of dense language about infrastructure, and her eyes skidded across it like tires on ice.

"Grandpa," she called down the hall, cupping her hand over the phone end, "did you vote on the water thing?"

He emerged in his cardigan, phone still going in his other ear, and held up one finger to his sister. "The water thing, the water thing." He came and stood at the counter and read the measure over Laurie's shoulder, lips moving slightly, which she found embarrassing for reasons she couldn't name. "You know how I got this?" he said, nodding at the laptop, at the ballot, at all of it. "Old enough to fight, old enough to vote. That was the slogan. Eighteen-year-olds could get drafted for the Vietnam War, so people said eighteen-year-olds should get to vote. That's why you're sitting there."

"I know the Twenty-Sixth Amendment," Laurie said, but softer than she'd planned, because she hadn't actually known the slogan, and there was something about hearing it in his voice, in the kitchen, that made it less like homework.

"You're the youngest person this family's ever had at that counter," he said. "Don't waste it being polite." He went back to his sister, who had apparently been holding forth the whole time.

Laurie looked at the screen. She thought about Caden, who was certain, and Margot, who was certain in the opposite direction, and her grandfather, who had been arguing since before she was born and seemed to think arguing was a form of love. She did not feel certain. She felt like she was holding two flashlights pointed at the same dark room, and each one lit a different half.

She voted for the water measure, because the dull government document about pipes had numbers in it she could check, and the Facebook post about scams had a font. Then she went back through the rest of the ballot, taking her time, and when she clicked submit, the little confirmation screen came up with a check mark so cheerful it looked sarcastic. Her father set down a plate of crackers with cheese on it beside her, wordless, and slid the lemon bar recipe tab to the front of her browser.

"There," he said. "Now that one has a right answer."

She laughed, and started measuring butter.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: CIRCLE, a research center at Tufts University, estimated that 50 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 voted in the 2020 presidential election.
story:
The envelope had been sitting on the desk since Tuesday, propped against the monitor like a dare. Jordyn turned eighteen three weeks ago, which meant that for the first time the county had mailed her a real ballot, her name typed in the little window, and she had responded by not touching it. Now it was Sunday evening, and the polls closed in two days, and her grandmother was asleep in the back room, convalescing slowly from the surgery, which meant the house was quiet enough to hear the refrigerator hum.

She slid the envelope under the desk lamp and logged on. Before she could pull up the voter guide, a message from Waylon appeared in their group chat.

You voting or what, he wrote. Mario says there's no point.

There is a point, Mario typed back a minute later. I'm just saying young people don't show up. Half of us don't even bother. My brother didn't. His friends didn't. Politicians know it, so they don't listen to us. Voting is like being the one person who shows up to a group project.

Jordyn frowned at that. Half felt both damning and vague, the kind of number people threw around the way Mario's brother called nonvoters couch slugs, a dysphemism that made it easy to dismiss everyone at once. She typed: where's that from.

It's just true, Mario wrote. Ask anyone.

Waylon sent: that's not a source, that's a vibe. Also Saturday, canvassing, I already signed us up. You're coming. Both of you.

Jordyn ignored the canvassing message for the moment, the way she ignored most things that arrived in capital letters. She opened a new tab and searched young people voted 2020. The first real result was from CIRCLE, a research center at Tufts University. They had estimated that 50 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 voted in the 2020 presidential election. She read it twice, then clicked through to the page itself to make sure some aggregator hadn't garbled it. Fifty percent. Mario's number was right, which surprised her, and so was his framing, which surprised her more, because the same number could be read the opposite way. Fifty percent of the largest young generation in decades was also tens of millions of ballots. The figure sat there in the middle of the screen like a coin that landed on its edge.

She thought about her grandmother, who had missed voting exactly once since 1968, the year she was in the hospital having Jordyn's mother. It wasn't a speech her grandmother had given; it was a story told over cardamom tea, one time, and Jordyn had mostly been watching the steam. Now it came back to her with unusual clarity.

She typed into the chat: ok so you're both kind of right. CIRCLE at Tufts estimated 50 percent of Americans 18 to 29 voted in 2020. Mario, that's your half. Waylon, that's also fifty percent of like forty-some million people, which is more than a lot of entire countries vote.

So it matters, Waylon wrote.

It matters and it doesn't, or it hasn't, Jordyn typed. I don't think either of you has a tenable position if you pretend it's simple. If we're half the story, we're also half missing.

Mario didn't answer for a while. The chat showed him typing, stopping, typing again. When his message finally came through it was longer than anything he usually sent. My brother says the local race is decided by like 300 votes, he wrote. School board. The one that closed the pool.

Jordyn looked at the ballot envelope. The school board race was on the back page, the one she'd been least interested in, names she hadn't looked up, and now it seemed like the heaviest part of the whole thing. She pulled the voter guide back up and found the two candidates, read their statements, read them again. One of them had a paragraph about the pool. She still wasn't sure about the county commissioner, or the judge retention questions, which seemed designed to be unanswered.

I'm doing the school board part for sure, she typed. The rest I'm figuring out tonight. And she underlined nothing and decided nothing else, but she did tear open the envelope, the paper ripping cleanly under the lamp, and carried the ballot to the kitchen table where the light was better.

Waylon's message arrived while she was finding a pen. Saturday, he wrote again. Nine a.m. I'm not asking.

Bring the clipboard, she wrote back. Mario?

A long pause. Then: fine, Mario sent. But I'm bringing coffee and I'm complaining the whole time.

She laughed out loud, once, in the quiet kitchen, and put her signature on the envelope flap.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Kahlo's The Broken Column (1944), her spine is painted as a cracked Ionic column visible through an opening in her body.
story:
Christian's grandmother kept the art books on the bottom shelf of the sunroom, between the birding guides and a box of photographs nobody opened anymore. He had come for the quiet, mostly, and because the apartment he shared with his mother felt too small the week before grades came out. Mr. Farah had assigned each of them one painting to tear apart before the semester ended. Christian had drawn Frida Kahlo's The Broken Column from the envelope, and the printout sat face-down on the tile table while he ate his grandmother's bread and olive oil.

"Turn it over, then," she said, setting down a second plate. "A picture doesn't do anything to you from the back."

He turned it over. The desert was striated ochre and green, the sky fissured with white cracks, and in the middle stood the woman with the sheet torn open down the front of her torso. Christian set his fork down without deciding to.

"That's the one with the column," his grandmother said. "She had the bus accident, the surgeries. Your grandfather liked her." She said it the way she mentioned him now, briefly, as if setting something small and breakable on the table between them. He had been dead since Christian was eleven, and Christian had never once heard her say what he liked about anything.

Zahra texted him around noon. Still stuck on mine. Yours is the easy one, it's famous. He typed back that famous wasn't the same as easy, and then, because that sounded like complaining, he asked what she saw in it. She replied with three words: the column first. Then a second message: why is architecture inside a body?

That question destabilized his whole outline. He had planned to write about the nails, the tears, the obvious catalog of pain, the essay everyone would write. But the nails were scattered all over the canvas, almost decorative, while the column stood dead centre, structural, load-bearing in a way that had nothing to do with flesh. He went back to the shelf and found the heavy Kahlo monograph, its spine soft from handling, and there was the painting again, larger, and there was his answer in the caption. Her spine is painted as a cracked Ionic column, visible through an opening in her body.

He read it aloud to his grandmother, feeling oddly like he was delivering news. "Ionic," she repeated, tasting the word. "The ones with the scrolls on top. Like the bank downtown." She leaned over the book. "So she is the building and the building is failing."

Marcel showed up at four with his bike and no helmet, having ridden the whole way from the east end. He was doing Monet, which he claimed was impossible to analyze because "it's just soup." He flopped into the other lawn chair and looked at the book only when Christian turned it toward him.

"It's weird that it's not the same as the cracks in the ground," Marcel said. "The landscape cracks go sideways. Hers goes straight up. Like a real column would."

Christian hadn't noticed that. He wrote it down and hated himself a little for not seeing it first, and then liked the note anyway, because the whole afternoon had that quality, every observation arriving with a small tax attached. The whites of the eyes versus the white of the corset. The green against the ochre, both of them desert colours, both of them hers. When he tried to say what the column meant, he kept circling: it was classical, it was ruined, it was holding something open rather than holding something up, it was inside her and it was her.

"You have to pick one reading," Marcel said. "Farah said pick one and defend it."

"Farah said that to you because you'd write soup otherwise." But Christian knew it was true of him too, that the assignment wanted a position and he had only a set of likenesses. He tried them out loud while his grandmother watered the geraniums. The column as the body's architecture. The column as everything outside the body that had broken it. The column as an older idea of woman, marble and white and split. Each one worked, which meant none of them worked on its own, and the honest essay would have to say so, which was the kind of essay that got a B.

His grandmother came back with two glasses of lemonade and stood behind his chair. "Your grandfather used to say she painted the inside on the outside because nobody would look at the inside otherwise." She set his glass down. "I don't know if that's criticism. He wasn't a critic."

Christian wrote it in the margin anyway, in the small handwriting he saved for things he hadn't decided about. Then he underlined the word inside twice and looked up at the sun going flat and orange over the neighbour's fence.

"So the tears," he said. "Are they because of the column, or separate?"

Marcel shrugged and drank his lemonade. "Write both. Say you can't tell."

"Farah wants discernment, not a shrug."

"Then shrug with vocabulary." Marcel grinned, and Christian, against his own better judgment, laughed and closed the book on top of the printout, keeping his page with his thumb.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: Ontario combines the federal GST with its provincial sales tax into a single 13 percent Harmonized Sales Tax, shown as one HST line on receipts.
story:
The waiting room of Patel & Associates smelled of toner and old carpet, and Joseph sat with his first paycheque flattened under his palm like something that might escape. His mother had insisted he come. Something about the numbers not looking right, and this being the year he learned what adults actually did every April. Across from him a man in a grey suit argued softly with the receptionist about mileage rates, and the fluorescent hum laid a kind of somnolence over everything, so that even the coffee in Joseph's cup seemed to be dozing.

"Joseph?" Ms. Campbell-Brown lived three doors down from him; he hadn't known she worked here, second desk by the window, reading glasses pushed up into her hair. She was also, inconveniently, his old accounting teacher from the semester he'd dropped the course. "You still owe me a unit on reconciliations."

"I still owe you an apology," he said, and she laughed and pulled his paycheque across the desk without asking, which was the whole reason his mother liked her.

She ran her finger down the stub. "Okay. Read me the top line." Gross pay. Then, beneath it, the deductions: federal income tax, provincial income tax, CPP, EI, each taking its small bite. He had known they would be there in the way you know a dentist will be there, abstractly, and then the drill arrives. "CPP is a pension," she said. "You're seventeen and you're already paying into a pension. EI is employment insurance, in case you're ever laid off." Net pay sat at the bottom, smaller and more honest than anything above it.

"It's like they're taking a cut of my money," he said.

"It's like you're buying things you can't buy alone," she said, but she said it lightly, and moved on before he could argue, which he suspected was a teaching habit she couldn't break.

What he hadn't told his mother, and what he had not quite told himself, was the real reason he was here. He had been the one collecting the lunch receipts for the robotics club's fundraiser dinner in Toronto last month. Forty-one dollars and forty-seven cents on the bill at the restaurant, and he had stared at it in the parking lot while Saige held the door, because there was only one tax line. One line, "HST," thirteen percent, no separate provincial charge. Every other receipt he'd ever seen at home in his mother's kitchen had two taxes stacked like stairs. He'd pocketed the receipt, told Saige the numbers were fine, and then spent three nights wondering if he'd been shortchanged, or if he'd shortchanged the club by claiming the wrong amount back.

Now he laid the receipt on Ms. Campbell-Brown's desk between two coffee rings. "In Toronto. Is this a mistake? Where's the other tax?"

She turned the paper toward the window light and was quiet long enough that he heard the man in the grey suit leave, the door sighing shut behind him. "Ontario combines the federal GST with the provincial sales tax into a single Harmonized Sales Tax," she said. "Thirteen percent, one HST line. That's the whole answer."

Joseph looked at the receipt again, at the single line he'd read a dozen times, feeling both stupid and relieved, the two feelings arriving together like guests who carpooled. "So the club wasn't overcharged."

"The club was charged exactly what everyone in Ontario pays on a restaurant meal." She handed it back. "Why did you think it was wrong?"

"Because at home everything has two lines." He paused. "And because I told Mila the reimbursement was off by six dollars and she went back through the whole envelope, and now she thinks I can't do arithmetic."

"Can you?"

"I equivocated," he admitted. "I told her maybe the restaurant made an error, and maybe Toronto was different, and honestly I was just hoping one of those was true."

Ms. Campbell-Brown took off her glasses entirely, which he remembered from class meant she was about to be either very kind or very direct. "Go home. Tell Mila what you told me, without the maybe. Then come back in April, when I'll show you a T4 and a return, and you'll watch most of that income tax come back to you, because you earned almost nothing. Deductions work both directions." She slid his paycheque across the desk. "You did the right thing eventually. That's the part that compounds."

He rode the bus home with the paycheque folded into his wallet, net pay uppermost, and texted Mila from the sidewalk outside the school. She was still in the building, rehearsal running late, and she came out the side door with her bag on one shoulder and her face arranged in the careful neutrality of someone prepared to be magnanimous.

"You found it," she said. "The mystery six dollars."

"There was no mystery. Ontario combines the GST and the provincial sales tax into one tax, thirteen percent, one line on the receipt. I didn't know that, and instead of saying so I was insouciant about it, which you correctly noticed, and then I wasn't insouciant at all, I was awake until one in the morning doing bad math."

Mila unzipped the envelope of receipts and held the restaurant bill up under the streetlight, her thumb covering the total. "One line," she said. "Huh." She looked at him over the top of it. "You're buying me fries for the three hours I spent on this."

"Thirteen percent tip," Joseph said, and held the door of the chip truck open for her.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Ontario requires most private residential landlords to use a government standard lease form for new leases, and a tenant can request one in writing if it was not provided.
story:
The laundromat on Elgin Street smelled like wet cotton and lemon detergent, and Hannah had spread two apartment leases across the folding table as if they were maps of the same country drawn by cartographers who hated each other. The dryer behind her thumped in a slow, arrhythmic way, like a heartbeat with something against it. She had a pencil, a calculator on her phone, and forty minutes until her laundry finished, which was exactly the amount of time she'd allotted herself to decide where she would live in September.

The first lease was for a room in a house near campus, six hundred a month plus a share of utilities, whatever "a share" meant, which the landlord had written as "to be divided fairly among tenants." The second was a one-bedroom over the laundromat itself, eight ninety a month, utilities included except hydro, which was a separate line, forty to seventy a month "depending on usage," which was another way of saying nothing at all. Hannah had exhumed both documents from the bottom of her backpack that morning, where they'd been softening under a water bottle and a bag of almonds for a week.

Olivia came in with her own basket, saw the papers, and set her laundry down two machines over, the way you'd give someone room at a crime scene. "Still deciding?"

"Still adding," Hannah said. "The second one is more per month but the first one has utilities on top, so I'm trying to figure out what 'a share of utilities' costs when there are four people and one of them takes half-hour showers."

"Ask him."

"He said 'don't worry about it.'"

Olivia dropped her detergent pod into the machine with the gravity of someone lighting a votive candle. "That's what my dad's landlord said about the leak, and then my dad's ceiling fell in."

Hannah looked back at the pages. That was when she noticed it, or rather noticed the absence of it. The second lease, the one over the laundromat, had a title page she'd skipped: it said Ontario Standard Form of Lease across the top, with a small government mark, and several pages of small print about the landlord's obligations. The first lease was two and a half pages, typed, with a clause that said the tenant waived certain rights, which Hannah had read three times because it seemed like the kind of sentence that should not be allowed to exist in a document you sign.

She texted August, who was the sort of person who read things for fun. Is there a rule about leases in Ontario? He answered nine minutes later, which for August was immediate: most private residential landlords have to use the government standard lease form for new leases. Then: if yours isn't one, you can ask for it in writing and they have to give it to you.

Hannah read that twice. She turned to Olivia. "Did you know there's a standard lease form? Like an official one the government makes."

"For what?"

"Most landlords here. For new leases. And if you didn't get one, you can request it in writing and they have to provide it." It came out flat, like she was reading a sign, which in a way she was.

Olivia leaned over, holding one wet sock like evidence. "So the house guy's two pages of 'don't worry about it'..."

"Isn't the standard form. No."

Mr. Kaminski, who ran the laundromat and owned, Hannah now realized, the apartment above it, came out from the back with a mop. He was maybe sixty, with a cardigan despite the heat, and he had a personal maxim he deployed at least once a visit, usually something like "dryers are honest, people are not." Today he stopped at the table and looked at the two leases without touching them.

"Comparing," he said.

"Trying to."

"The one upstairs is the standard form," he said. "I printed it off the government site. Took me an hour to fill in properly. My lawyer friend said my old one from ten years ago was, his word, deleterious. Bad for both of us, apparently. Mine had a no-guests clause. Not enforceable, but it sat there being believed."

Hannah thought about the clause she'd read three times, the waiver of rights, sitting there being believed. She had been leaning toward the cheaper room all week. Six hundred a month was six hundred a month, and her mother had said, more than once, that rent was rent and everything else was vanity. But the math she'd been doing all morning was the wrong math, or at least an incomplete math. The house's true cost wasn't six hundred plus a share of utilities. It was six hundred plus utilities plus whatever the two and a half pages were quietly taking from her, some of which she couldn't price because she didn't yet know what it was called.

"I'm going to email him," she said. "Ask in writing for the standard form."

"Then you'll see," Mr. Kaminski said, and went back to mopping.

"See what?" Olivia asked.

"How he answers. If it's fine, then the numbers are the numbers and maybe I take the cheap room. If it's not fine..." She didn't finish, because she didn't know yet what the end of that sentence was, and she was tired of pretending she did.

The dryer buzzed. Hannah gathered the leases, squared them against the table edge, and slid them into her backpack with more care than they'd received all week, the standard form on top. Then she opened her phone, started a new email to the landlord of the house on Regent Street, and typed, "I'm writing to request the standard lease form."

"Signing it?" Olivia asked.

"After he answers."

The washing machine behind them clicked into its spin cycle, and Hannah's thumbs hovered over the send button.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: During Chuseok, Korea's harvest festival on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month, many families hold charye, a memorial rite that sets out food for their ancestors.
story:
Laurence stood at the kitchen counter with her grandmother's notebook open to a page of Hangul she could not read and a diagram she could: a rectangle for the table, arrows pointing to where each dish belonged. Her mother had handed it over three days ago with the words "You're doing it this year," and then left for work, as though that settled everything. It did not settle anything. In two days the apartment would fill with aunts and cousins, and the table would have to be right, because the table was the whole thing.

"This one goes where?" Marcus leaned over her shoulder, holding a printout from a website about Korean holidays. He had offered to help, though what he mostly did was eat the fried tofu she was supposed to save for the offering.

"Row three, west side. Fruits go west." She tapped the diagram. "I think."

"You think."

"That's why we're checking." She flattened the printout beside the notebook. The website said Chuseok was Korea's harvest festival, that it fell on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, and that many families held charye, a memorial rite that set out food for their ancestors. She read it twice. Her grandmother had never used the word charye in front of her, or if she had, it had gone past, lost in the stream of a language Laurence understood only at the level of food and scolding.

The trouble was the gap between the two documents. The diagram showed five rows, each with its own logic, meat on one side, fish on the other, rice and soup nearest the spirits' place at the north end. The website gave the reasoning behind each placement, and the reasoning contradicted the diagram in two places. In the notebook, pears sat on the east; online, fruit belonged west. Her grandmother had either done it differently from everyone else, or the notebook had been copied wrong forty years ago and the error had transmuted, over decades of repetition, into family custom indistinguishable from law.

"I could text Maurice," Marcus said. "His stepmom's Korean."

"She's from Busan. We're not. Whatever she does could be a Busan thing." Laurence pulled the pear bowl toward the east edge of the counter, then pushed it back. "Grandma didn't do a Busan thing. She did her thing."

"So do her thing."

"Her thing is in a language I can't read, and the picture fights the internet, and everybody coming on Thursday has an opinion." She could already hear her aunt, who treated every family gathering as a small oligarchy with herself at the top, announcing that the chestnuts were placed by someone who clearly didn't know better. Her cousin would film it. There would be a group chat.

She carried her phone down the hall and knocked on Mr. Yip's door. He was the neighbor who had lived in the building longer than anyone and who had watched her grandmother carry groceries up four flights for fifteen years. He answered in his slippers, wiping his hands on a towel.

"Mr. Yip, did my grandmother ever talk to you about the holiday table? Chuseok. The memorial rite. She set out food for the ancestors every year."

He looked at her for a moment. "She talked about the pears once. She said in her mother's house the fruit went east, and her husband's family put it west, and she'd married into their way but kept the east for the pears anyway. She thought it was funny. Like a small rebellion."

Laurence stood in the doorway holding the pear bowl, which she had brought without deciding to. So the notebook was not wrong and it was not the family way either. It was one woman's quiet amendment, kept so long that the amendment had become the family way, and now it was hers to keep or lose.

Marcus was waiting in the kitchen with the tofu plate half empty. "So?" he said.

"West for everything, east for the pears." She set the bowl on the counter's east side. "That's the answer, or it's my answer, and if my aunt says the pears are wrong, she can argue with a dead woman about it."

"Harsh."

"Accurate." She began stacking the small white dishes from the cupboard, counting them out to the north end of the table, then stopped at five and recounted. Marcus slid the last piece of tofu across the counter toward her, and she took it before he could change his mind.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In a 2011 Stanford study, basketball players who aimed for 10 hours in bed nightly improved their free-throw average from 7.9 to 8.8 successful shots out of 10.
story:
Sienna taped the grid to the chain-link behind the backstop, seven columns wide, one for each day, and stood back to look at it like a painter checking proportion. Monday said arm care and long toss. Tuesday said rest, which she had written in small letters, as though the word might apologize for itself. Enzo arrived first, cleats slung over one shoulder, and read the grid upside down.

"You gave Thursday nothing," he said. "Two rest days. You're planning to be injured or something?"

"I'm planning to not be injured."

Anas came across the outfield grass with a lacrosse ball he kept squeezing in his left hand, a habit nobody commented on anymore. He read the grid right side up, which gave him an advantage over Enzo, and tapped Tuesday with the lacrosse ball. "Rest is training," he said. "My sister's physio says that."

"My coach says the ones who lionize the grind end up in his office by July," Sienna said. She said it lightly, but she had been in that office in August, junior year, her shoulder hot and useless, while Mr. Bear, who taught chemistry and kept the field schedule, had said very little and handed her the ice pack himself.

They warmed up the way the grid demanded now, which annoyed Enzo, who preferred to walk onto a field already at full speed, a mercurial quality that made him brilliant some days and, on others, made him sprint after a fly ball with cold hamstrings and pull up short, cursing at the basepath. Today was a brilliant day, or started as one. He shagged two over the fence in left, showboating the second one, one-handed. Sienna threw her bullpen sequence, marked the sheet, and noticed Anas yawning into his glove between pitches.

"You were up until two again," she said.

"Stats homework." He shrugged. "Then I couldn't stop watching this pitcher in Korea. He has a slide step that's honestly illegal looking."

Sienna had a binder, and the binder had a page she'd found at one in the morning herself, which was a fact she was keeping to herself. The page was about a 2011 Stanford study. Basketball players, aiming for ten hours in bed nightly, had improved their free-throw average from 7.9 to 8.8 successful shots out of 10. She had read it twice, then read it again, because her first reaction was that a number had been misprinted, and her second reaction was that the players hadn't changed anything she would have called training at all. No drill, no coach, no new mechanic. Just bed.

"Anas," she said. "If I told you a pitcher could get better without throwing one extra pitch, would you do it?"

"Depends what it is."

"Sleep. Ten hours in bed, every night. That's the whole thing." She told him the numbers, 7.9 to 8.8 out of 10, and watched him do the same arithmetic she had done, the small and slightly insulting arithmetic where rest outranked half her drill block.

"Free throws aren't pitching," he said, which was fair, and she said she knew that, which was also fair, and neither of them mentioned that the binder page said 2011, Stanford, as if a study needed a birth certificate to be believed. The trouble was that Anas liked being up at two in the morning the way some people liked the ocean, and Sienna could not tell whether the study's promise was worth more than that. She was honest enough with herself to leave the question open.

Mr. Bear unlocked the equipment shed at four, as always, and paused at the taped grid on his way past. He looked at Tuesday and Thursday, the small apologetic letters, and at the bottom row where Sienna had written in a sleep column, ten hours, with a question mark after it on Saturday.

"The question mark's honest," he said.

"That's the pragmatics of it," Sienna said, borrowing the word from her linguistics reading, where it meant the difference between what a sentence says and what a person does with it. "I can write ten hours. Whether I'll be in bed at ten is a separate fact about the world."

He laughed once through his nose and went into the shed, and she heard the rake handles settle against the wall. Enzo was still in left field, lying flat on his back in the grass with his glove over his face, and Anas was standing at the mound with the ball in his hand, looking at the horizon in the direction of his own bedroom window.

"Ten hours," he called out. "Starting tonight. You're my witness."

Sienna uncapped the marker and, under Saturday, replaced the question mark with a small check mark she could always cross out later. Then she picked up her glove and ran out to the outfield, where the grass was still damp and smelled like rain that hadn't happened yet.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In countries where tax is withheld from pay, such as the US and Canada, a tax refund means more was withheld during the year than was owed; it is an overpayment returned, not extra income.
story:
Tristan had wanted the bicycle since March, a used one listed online for two hundred and forty dollars, and by June he had saved most of it from his job at the hardware store. His first paycheque had confused him. He had expected the number he'd been quoted per hour times his hours, and instead the deposit was smaller, with a stub showing lines he hadn't asked for. Federal income tax withheld. Provincial sales tax he didn't see on the stub at all, but he saw it everywhere else: on the receipt for work gloves, on the receipt for the chain lube he'd bought in April, a percentage added at the till so that a $9.99 item rang up over eleven dollars. He had started keeping the receipts in a shoebox without quite deciding to.

On the Thursday before Canada Day he sat at the kitchen computer to transfer the last of the money. The banking page loaded slowly, and while it did, a message came in from Clark: at the bank with his cousin, who had just gotten her tax refund, eight hundred dollars, and she was calling it free money, taking everyone out for ice cream. Tristan typed congratulations, put the phone face down, and stared at the progress bar.

He had filed his own return that spring, a simple one, because Ms. Sokolov had mentioned in passing that even students with small incomes should file. He'd used the software, entered the number from the box on his slip, the total tax withheld from all his paycheques, and the program had told him he was getting back sixty-one dollars. At the time he'd treated it like a small windfall and bought a better lock for his current bike. Now, waiting for the page to load, he opened the return again and looked at it properly.

The software showed two figures side by side: the amount withheld during the year and the amount he actually owed. The second number was smaller. The refund was the difference. He leaned back and let that settle. Nothing had been given to him; his cousin of Clark's, the one with the eight hundred dollars, had simply had more taken off her cheques during the year than she ended up owing, and the government was returning the difference. It was an overpayment, he thought, not income. He said the word aloud once, quietly, to hear whether it fit. It did.

He picked the phone back up. You know that's not extra money, right, he typed. It was her own pay, held back all year and given back.

Clark replied three minutes later with a photo of a waffle cone and the words she doesn't care, it feels like a bonus. Tristan set the phone down again without answering. He understood the feeling; the sixty-one dollars had felt like a bonus to him too, back in April, when he spent it. But sitting here now, with the return open on one half of the screen and the bicycle listing on the other, the two ways of thinking sat uneasily together. The refund was real money, spendable, arriving at a useful moment, and it was also, in some plainer sense, not new money at all. He tried to hold both of those at once and found they didn't cancel out. They just coexisted, like knowing a photograph was staged and finding it beautiful anyway.

The banking page finally loaded. He entered the transfer: one hundred and ninety dollars to savings, which with what was there already would clear the two hundred and forty, plus the sales tax he'd have to pay the seller if they met at a shop for the tune-up. His mother passed through the kitchen and asked if he'd eaten. He said yes. She stood behind him a moment, looking at the screen, and asked why he had his tax return open. He said he was checking something, and she went to the fridge without asking what. Something in her not asking made him sit straighter, as though the checking were now official.

He messaged Priscilla, who had the same job at a different store, and asked what her stub showed. She sent a photo of it, taken crooked on a break room table: gross pay at the top, then the deductions under it, each one a small subtraction, then the net deposit at the bottom, the only number that ever reached her account. He looked at his own stub from two weeks ago and compared the lines. The withheld income tax was there, sitting between what he'd earned and what he'd been paid, like a fee held in trust rather than a fee paid. He would find out at the end of the year, when he added it all up, whether the holding had been exact. Last year it hadn't been. That was all a refund was.

Later that evening he ruminated on it while the torpid heat of the apartment made thinking feel like moving through water. He didn't want to tell Clark his cousin was wrong in a way that would spoil the ice cream, but he also didn't want to be the kind of person who let a thing slide just because correcting it cost something. The compromise he arrived at, which he didn't fully trust, was that he'd mention it once, without insisting, the next time it came up naturally. If it never came up naturally, he would let it go. He couldn't decide whether that was discretion or cowardice, and he suspected it was both.

Clark messaged at ten. Cousin says thanks for ruining ice cream, apparently someone else told her the same thing. Then, after a pause: she says at least it's still eight hundred dollars. Tristan typed back, it's her own eight hundred, and put the phone in the shoebox on top of the receipts, screen up so he'd hear it if she answered.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Philosopher Stephen Toulmin, in his 1958 book The Uses of Argument, described an argument's backbone as a claim, the grounds or data supporting it, and a warrant explaining why those grounds support the claim.
story:
The seminar room smelled of dry-erase marker and someone's microwaved noodles, and Mr. Harper had already pushed the desks into their crooked circle before anyone arrived. Maika sat with her persuasive essay draft flat on the table, its margins crowded with arrows, and listened to Shayne argue that the school should fund the robotics team before the theater program. Konnor, who had built the set for last fall's play, was obdurate about it, arms crossed, repeating that the stage lights were a fire hazard and the administration knew it.

"Your evidence is three fundraising shortfalls," Shayne said, tapping his phone. "I have enrollment numbers. Twice as many students want engineering electives."

"So you're saying numbers beat safety," Konnor said.

Maika had stopped hearing the argument itself. She was staring at her own draft, her claim circled twice in blue ink, her facts listed underneath it like loyal soldiers, and something about the arrangement felt false. The essay argued that the city should keep the public pool open through winter, and she had plenty of grounds: attendance figures, a petition with four hundred names, a study about swim programs and youth fitness. Mr. Harper had written one comment at the bottom, in pencil. You never tell me why these support your claim.

The problem had gnawed at her for two days. It was like owning all the ingredients for a meal and no recipe, like having bricks stacked on a lot with no mortar between them. Around the circle, Mr. Harper was now asking Shayne to slow down, and Maika half-heard Shayne flip his notebook open to a page he'd copied from somewhere.

"Okay, so I read this for my outline," Shayne said. "The philosopher Stephen Toulmin, in his 1958 book The Uses of Argument, described an argument's backbone as a claim, the grounds or data supporting it, and a warrant explaining why those grounds support the claim."

Mr. Harper nodded but said nothing, which was his way of handing the room over.

"A warrant," Konnor repeated, squinting. "Like a guarantee?"

"Like the bridge," Shayne said. "The part that connects them."

Maika's pen went still. Bridge. That was the missing thing, and it had a name she hadn't known to look for. Her essay assumed that if four hundred people signed a petition, the council should therefore act, but she had never once written that assumption down. Maybe the council believed petitions were subterfuge, organized noise rather than conviction. Maybe attendance figures could be transmuted into an argument for a private contractor instead of a public commitment. Her grounds could be steered toward a conclusion she hated if she left the steering unwritten. The warrant wasn't decoration; it was the place where the argument could be attacked, which meant it was also the place where it could be defended.

"Maika," Mr. Harper said, and she looked up too fast. "You've been quiet. You had the pool essay, yes?"

"I think I found the problem," she said. Her voice came out uneven, and she let it. "My evidence is fine. I never wrote the warrant. The part that says why the petition counts, why attendance means the pool should stay open. If I don't say that out loud, someone else gets to invent it for me."

Konnor leaned forward, chin off his fist. "So what's your warrant? That the city should serve whoever shows up?"

"Maybe," Maika said. "But that's the hard part, actually. What if the people who show up are only the ones with time to sign things? Then my own grounds could undercut me." She heard the sentence leave her mouth and recognized it as the first honest thing she'd said about the essay all week. It would be easier if the warrant were obvious. It wasn't. It was a conditional, a chain of ifs: if the petition represents the neighborhood, and if representation should move budgets, then the pool stays open. Each if was a door someone could walk through and argue from the other side.

Shayne turned his notebook toward her. "Toulmin has more parts than that, apparently. Rebuttals. Qualifiers."

"Don't tell me yet," Maika said, and she laughed a little at her own seriousness. "Let me be wrong on my own first."

Mr. Harper checked the clock, then didn't call time. Konnor had gone back to the stage lights, and Shayne was drafting a warrant about safety in green ink, crossing it out twice. Maika pulled her essay closer and began writing in the narrow space under the pencil comment, small and deliberate: if the pool is the only winter water access in this district, then attendance is not a convenience but a need.

She read the line over once, then a second time, and underlined it.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Hormonal IUDs and contraceptive implants fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once placed by a clinician they do not depend on daily use.
story:
Gabriella had the pamphlets fanned across her lap like a bad hand of cards when Skye finally texted back. Waiting room's the worst part, Skye wrote, followed by three nauseated faces. Gabriella typed "you can do this" and deleted it, because Skye hated being encouraged, and instead wrote "I'm in the waiting room too." That part was true. What she hadn't said was why she was there.

They had been assigned as partners for the peer health program at school, the one Ms. Reyes ran out of the library on Thursdays. The assignment was to operationalize a set of ideas, Ms. Reyes's phrase, until the ideas became something a person could actually do: how to say yes and how to say no and how to mean either one, what protection existed and how well it worked, where to go for testing and what happened when you got there. Ms. Reyes wanted them to practice on each other until the words stopped sounding rehearsed. "You'll be explaining this to people who are scared," she had said, "so you'd better not be." Gabriella had taken that seriously. Skye had taken it as an excuse to make jokes about bananas.

But that morning Skye had asked, in a voice with no jokes in it, whether Gabriella knew where the clinic was, and whether you needed an appointment, and whether they'd tell your parents. So now Gabriella sat in the beige waiting room with the pamphlets, rehearsing consent out loud in a murmur, like a liturgy. Enthusiastic, ongoing, yours to withdraw. The fluorescent light made everything look like evidence.

The nurse called Skye's name first. Through the half-open door Gabriella caught fragments: a question about the last menstrual period, a pause that went on long enough to have a shape. Then the door closed, and Gabriella turned to the second pamphlet, the one about methods, because she realized she didn't actually know the numbers. She had been planning to say "most methods work pretty well," which was the kind of equivocal sentence that helped nobody. If she was going to explain this to scared people, she needed facts with edges.

At the front desk, she asked the receptionist, who printed a comparison chart, and then, when the chart's fine print defeated her, Gabriella leaned toward the triage window where a nurse was filing folders. "Can I ask you something for a school thing?" The nurse waved her over. Gabriella pointed at the row for the implant and the hormonal IUD and asked why their failure numbers were so much lower than the pill's. "Because once a clinician places them, they don't depend on you remembering anything day to day," the nurse said, tapping the row. "Fewer than 1 in 100 users a year get pregnant on them. The pill only works like that if you take it perfectly, and people don't." Gabriella wrote it down word for word, her pen pressing through the paper. That was the sentence she'd hand people. Not pretty well. Fewer than one in a hundred, and it doesn't depend on you being perfect every single morning.

She was still copying when the chair beside hers scraped, and Brooke sat down. Brooke, who had a boyfriend at the state school, Brooke, who had once said in the locker room that girls who needed the clinic were sloppy. Brooke had her sleeves pulled over her hands and her eyes fixed on the fish tank, where an angelfish was eating something too small to see. "Don't," Brooke said, before Gabriella could speak.

"I'm not going to say anything."

"You're here for the peer thing. Everyone knows about Thursdays."

"I'm here for Skye," Gabriella said, and watched that land, and then, because the information was hers to use now, she slid the comparison chart across the armrest. "That's the thing I didn't know until ten minutes ago. The implant and the IUD, fewer than one in a hundred a year, because once they're in they don't depend on daily use. If you're deciding anything, that's the number I'd start with." Brooke looked at the chart and not at her. Gabriella thought of Ms. Reyes saying the program wasn't a meritocracy, that nobody earned a scare, and she understood it now in a way she hadn't on Thursday.

The exam room door opened and Skye came out fast, buttoning her coat wrong, one side longer than the other. "It's negative," Skye said, too loud for the room, and a man by the fish tank glanced over. Then, quieter, "But I got tested. Everything. They just took blood and, like, swabbed my throat. I didn't know you had to ask for the throat one." She was crying a little and grinning at the same time, which was the most honest face Gabriella had ever seen her make.

"We should put that in the presentation," Gabriella said, standing, gathering the pamphlets. "The asking part. How to ask."

"Brooke can do the demo," Skye said, and Brooke said, "Shut up," but she was folding the chart into her pocket, along the creases, carefully, like something she meant to keep.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: A force majeure clause frees the parties from their obligations when an extraordinary event outside their control, such as a natural disaster or war, prevents them from performing.
story:
The rain had been coming down since Tuesday, and by Friday afternoon the parking lot of the Harborline Arena had become a shallow brown lake with islands of shopping carts. Lauren stood at the box office window of Mr. Georgiou's ticket agency, watching a woman in a raincoat argue with the girl at the next window, and wished, not for the first time, that she had taken the coffee shop job instead.

She had been here since June, after graduation, folding flyers for the Cosmopolitan Orchestra's summer series and learning the grammar of the business: terms, conditions, liability, the small print that customers never read and always blamed her for. Mr. Georgiou liked to say that a ticket was a promise folded into paper, and that promises had edges. She had liked that, at first. It captivated her, the idea that a whole relationship between a buyer and a band could live inside eight point font.

At four o'clock Hilary came through the door shaking water off her jacket, holding her phone out like evidence. "They canceled it," she said. "The Saturday show. The venue flooded, the whole stage is under two inches of water, they just posted it."

Lauren already knew. Mr. Georgiou had called her an hour ago, his voice tight, telling her to pull the ticket stock and wait for instructions before issuing any refunds. The Saturday show had sold four hundred and twelve tickets through the agency alone, and the money sat in the agency account until settlement day, which was Monday.

"So I get my money back," Hilary said. It wasn't quite a question. She had bought six tickets, for herself and Lyndon and four others from the swim team, out of her own account, on the promise they would pay her back. Sixty dollars each. Lauren did the math and did not say it out loud.

"There's a clause," Lauren said slowly. She pulled a ticket from the drawer and turned it over, and there in the gray block of print, between the parking disclaimer and the recording policy, was the phrase she had typed into her phone two weeks ago when a customer had asked about it: FORCE MAJEURE. She had looked it up then, out of boredom, on a slow Wednesday. A force majeure clause frees the parties from their obligations when an extraordinary event outside their control, such as a natural disaster or war, prevents them from performing.

"Which means what?" Hilary asked.

"It's French," Lauren said. "Sort of. 'Superior force.'" She was buying time and knew it, because the clause cut both ways, and she wasn't yet sure which way it cut here.

Lyndon arrived at five, dripping, still in his lifeguard windbreaker. He wanted the refund money tonight, not Monday, not next week, because his car payment was due Sunday and he had floated Hilary's bus fare to the meet in April and everything in his life was a loan against something else. He leaned on the counter and laid out the case with the flat certainty he used for everything: the flood canceled the show, the show didn't happen, the money comes back. Simple.

But it wasn't simple, and that was the part Lauren couldn't stop turning over. If the flood freed the promoter from having to perform the concert, it might also free the promoter from having to refund. The clause said the parties, plural. She had the terms page open under the counter, and the more she read, the more the sentence seemed to face both directions at once, like an isthmus you could walk down from either coast and arrive somewhere different depending on where you started.

Mr. Georgiou came back at six, carrying a folder of settlement papers, and stood in the doorway listening to the rain hammer the awning. "The promoter says the money moves Monday," he said. "They invoked the clause. No obligations until then."

"They can't just keep it," Lyndon said.

"They can wait with it," Mr. Georgiou said. "Which for you is the same thing until it isn't."

Hilary looked at Lauren across the counter, and Lauren understood that her friend was asking her to choose, not between right and wrong, but between the promise the ticket made and the promise the paper carved out of it. She thought of the four hundred buyers, the four hundred signatures nobody remembered making when they clicked accept, the consent that lived in a checkbox. Then she thought of the girl at the next window, still arguing, getting nowhere with sympathy.

"The clause frees both sides," Lauren said. "Fine. Then we're freed too. The agency's not holding their money hostage, we're holding it in trust until performance, and performance just became impossible. So we refund from the agency account tonight and settle with the promoter Monday, and if they fight it, they fight it with Mr. Georgiou, not with a swim team."

Mr. Georgiou looked at her for a long moment, rain streaming down the glass behind him. "That's the agency's money until Monday," he said. "If the promoter goes under, you're spending my savings."

"If we don't, we're spending their trust," Lauren said. "Pick which one you can get back."

He set the folder on the counter, unlocked the drawer, and slid the refund pad toward her. "Sixty each," he said. "And you stay until the last one walks out the door."

Lauren wrote the first refund while Lyndon texted the swim team and Hilary counted out the cash drawer twice, and at nine forty that night, when the window finally came down, the rain had stopped and the parking lot had gone still and mirror-flat, holding the streetlights in long silver columns all the way to the curb.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear.
story:
Brayden's list, folded twice in his jacket pocket, was almost ascetic in its economy: onions, carrots, celery, a carton of broth, one loaf of bread. His mother had texted him from her shift at the hospital, "soup??? you're a lifesaver," and he had decided to take the compliment literally, or at least seriously, which for Brayden meant following a recipe the way other people followed scripture. He was standing in the produce aisle comparing two yellow onions when Judith found him, having abandoned her own basket somewhere near the yogurt.

"You're holding them like they're going to confess," she said. She picked up the bigger one and put it in his basket before he could object. "More onion. Your whole family is going to fight over this soup and you want to be stingy?"

"I'm not stingy, I'm precise. There's a difference."

"You're doctrinaire," said Judith, with the pleasure of someone deploying a word she'd learned that week in English. "You follow the recipe like it's the law. Cooking is more like jazz."

"Cooking is chemistry," said Brayden, and immediately regretted it, because Judith had taken chemistry with him last year and had never once let him forget the incident with the overturned burner. At the checkout, the cashier scanned his vegetables without ceremony, and Brayden kept one eye on the total, subtracting it from the twenty his mother had left under the magnet on the fridge. The bread went in last, warm from the bakery section, and Judith carried it out to the bus stop cradled in both arms like a small sleeping animal.

Judith had insisted on coming along to help, partly out of kindness and partly, she suspected, because her own house that afternoon contained only her father's watching of golf and a refrigerator empty except for condiments. She liked Brayden's kitchen, which smelled of the spices his mother kept in mismatched jars, and she liked the project of it, the peeling and the chopping, the way an evening could be built out of small concrete tasks. She took the onion duty because Brayden announced he would handle the knife work with "surgical focus," and she wanted to see whether that was true.

It was not, or it was, and the onion got its revenge anyway. Halfway through the dicing, her eyes began to flood, and then to burn, and she turned away from the cutting board blinking fast. Brayden looked up from arranging his carrots by size and grinned.

"Are you crying?"

"I am not crying. It's the onion." She wiped her face with her sleeve and kept chopping, which made it worse. "It's a chemical thing. Cutting it breaks the cells and releases enzymes, and they make this vapor, syn-propanethial-S-oxide. It goes in your eyes and you tear up. Everybody does. Look it up if you don't believe me."

He did look it up, phone propped against the flour canister, and read it twice, and felt the specific small embarrassment of a person who has teased someone about a fact he himself did not know. He had been ready to excoriate her for sentimentality over a vegetable, and instead the vegetable was simply waging chemical warfare on both of them, indifferent to character. He took the knife to prove a point and lasted maybe forty seconds before his own eyes were streaming.

"Okay," he said, wiping his face on a dish towel, laughing at himself. "Okay. You were right and I was obnoxious. Both things can be true."

"Both things are definitely true," said Judith. She slid the chopping board toward the pot and he swept the onions in, and they hit the oil with a hiss that filled the kitchen, and she thought that this, the hiss and the smell and the absurd stinging eyes, was better than jazz or chemistry, though she would never tell him so, because he would only get doctrinaire about that too.

Later, when his mother came home and stood in the doorway with her coat still on, sniffing the air, Brayden set out four bowls and did not say the soup was ready, exactly; he said, "We made it. Both of us. I did the carrots." Judith, from the stove, held up the ladle like a conductor's baton, and the steam rose between them, carrying the smell of onions all the way to the front door.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note one octave higher than another vibrates at exactly twice its frequency, so the A above A440 is 880 hertz.
story:
The violin had belonged to Mya's grandfather, and it had sat in the back closet of her grandmother's house for six years before anyone thought to open the case again. Mya's grandmother brought it out on a Tuesday in July, set it on the kitchen table, and said nothing about it for an hour, which was her way of asking.

Mya had wanted an instrument of her own for most of high school, something she could carry to college in the fall, but the plan had always been vague, a someday thing, and she had let it stay vague. Now the instrument was in front of her, smelling of rosin and dust, and the vague plan had a shape whether she was ready for it or not. That first week she learned to hold it without her left wrist collapsing, and the sound she made was so ugly that she closed the windows before she practiced, out of a sense of responsibility, almost of culpability, as if the neighbors were being made to pay for her education.

Ms. Ho lived next door, in the house with the row of wind chimes, and she was the one who had suggested the tuner app. She had heard the scraping through the walls, knocked on the screen door with a plate of sesame cookies, and said, "You'll want to know when you're in tune. Your grandfather never did, and it drove everyone at his church crazy." What Ms. Ho wanted, Mya understood gradually, was for the violin to be played again, and preferably in public. She asked every few days whether Mya might join the little ensemble at her church, and Mya said each time, honestly, that she was nowhere near good enough, though she suspected that "good enough" meant something different at a small church than it did anywhere else, something less parochial than her own standards, oddly enough, and more forgiving.

The tuner was a small green line on her phone screen that bent left or right with every turn of the pegs. Mya learned to chase it. She got the A string steady at 440, a number she had seen printed on the app's face without thinking much about it, and then one afternoon, running her fingers up the string for practice, she stopped on a note that sounded like the same A, only brighter, and glanced at the screen. The number read 880. She moved her finger back down and played the open string. 440. Up again. 880. She did this four times, feeling slightly ridiculous, like someone checking that a light switch still worked.

She texted Carley, who had taken physics the year before. "is the app broken or does the higher A actually vibrate twice as fast." Carley answered from her lifeguarding shift with a photo of the pool and one line: "yeah, an octave up is exactly double. 440 to 880. it's not broken." Mya sat on her grandmother's porch steps with the phone against her knee and the violin across her lap, and it seemed strange to her that the same note, the same letter, could be two different numbers at once, and stranger still that the doubling was exact, not close, not approximate, but exactly twice, as if the universe had decided on one clean rule and kept it. She had assumed music was fuzzy, a matter of taste, and here was a part of it that behaved like arithmetic.

She began testing other notes to see if the pattern held everywhere, which it did not in any simple way she could find, and that interested her even more. The fact of the doubled A gave her a place to stand, a fixed point, and from there she could feel out the rest, but she could not yet say why some intervals sounded warm and others sounded like a door argument. There were two ways of thinking in her head now, the counting way and the listening way, and she did not want to give up either of them. She suspected they would meet somewhere, eventually, in some understanding she did not yet have, and she was honest enough with herself to admit she might be wrong about that too.

The practicing catalyzed something in her grandmother's house. The piano in the front room got opened and dusted, though no one played it. Old sheet music appeared in a stack by the couch. Her grandmother started humming while she cooked, quietly, in the key Mya happened to be practicing in, as though the sound had let something else into the air.

In August, Ms. Ho knocked again, this time without cookies, holding a photocopied flyer for the ensemble's September evening service. "They lost their second violin," she said. "It's simple music. Half notes, whole notes." Mya looked at the flyer, then at the violin case by the door, which she had begun to think of as hers, though no one had said so. "I'd have to practice the octave jumps," she said. "The 880 ones." Ms. Ho folded her hands. "Then practice them," she said. Mya took the flyer and set it on the piano, on the stack of her grandfather's music, and went to get the case.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The overall equation for aerobic cellular respiration is C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy: glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water.
story:
Alice had promised herself she would learn cellular respiration by sunset, and the sun was already leaning on the treetops around Raven's Pond, which was turbid that evening, the color of weak tea with opinions.

"So you brought flashcards to a body of water," Raven said, dropping onto the log beside her. "Bold."

"It's quiet here. Home is not quiet. Home is my little brother discovering the trombone."

"That's fair. That's a real threat." Raven peeled the tab off a can of soda and flicked it into the grass, where Alice retrieved it, because she was that kind of person and Raven tolerated it.

The exam was first period tomorrow. Mr. Hassan had announced it on Friday with the cheerful menace of a man handing out parking tickets: "It will cover everything from glycolysis to the electron transport chain, and yes, I expect the overall equation." Alice had written it on an index card that morning, stared at it, and understood it about as well as she understood the trombone. The card said glucose plus oxygen becomes carbon dioxide plus water plus energy, and somewhere in the middle of that sentence were the mitochondria, doing whatever they did, cheerfully, at her expense.

"Quiz me," she said.

"You're the biology person."

"I'm a biology person who is failing to be a biology person. Quiz me anyway. Read the card."

Raven held it up, squinting theatrically. "C6H12O6 plus six O2 yields six CO2 plus six H2O plus energy. Okay, so sugar plus oxygen."

"That much I have. Sugar and oxygen go in."

"And carbon dioxide and water come out, plus energy. It's like a receipt. You pay in donuts and breathing, you get burps and energy."

"That's not what it's like at all," Alice said, and then stopped, because actually it was a little what it was like. A receipt. An accounting. Glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water, and the energy, the ATP, is the disbursement that underwrites everything else, every step of it happening in the mitochondria, which her textbook called, embarrassingly, the powerhouse of the cell. She had always hated that phrase. It sounded like a poster in a dentist's office.
