But sitting here with the pond going dark and the exam coming bright, she thought she finally saw what it was reaching for: a budget, a flow, a way matter moved through you and paid you back in motion.

"Where does the carbon go, though," she said, mostly to herself.

"The carbon?"

"In the sugar. Six carbons go in, six come out as CO2. I breathe them out. Every time I exhale, I'm exhaling yesterday's pasta."

Raven considered this with visible seriousness, which was Raven's way of mocking her while also being interested. "So right now I'm breathing on you and it's carbon dioxide from my lunch."

"Technically, and also gross, yes."

"I had a bagel. You're welcome." Raven breathed on her, deliberately, with ceremony.

"Thank you for your donation of water vapor and bagel carbon." Alice flipped the card over, where she'd written the whole thing out again in pencil, twice, because writing things twice was supposed to underwrite remembering them, and so far had underwritten only hand cramps. C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy. The arrows had begun to look like little ponds themselves.

"Okay but here's my question," Raven said. "The mitochondria. Are they, like, yours? Do you own them?"

"Inherited from my mom, actually. All of them, every last one, down the maternal line. There's a whole thing about it."

"So when you ace this exam, technically your mom gets partial credit."

"I'll be sure to mention that to Mr. Hassan. He'll love a maternal lineage argument on a test about ATP."

"It's called hedging your grade."

Alice laughed, and then, in the way of evenings, the laughing made room for the worrying again. She looked at the pond, at the duckweed crowding the near shore, at the water doing its slow green business. Somewhere in that turbid soup, things were respiring too, taking in oxygen, letting out carbon dioxide, all of it invisible and all of it exactly the shape of the equation on her card. The world was full of the receipt. She just had to be able to read it by 8:25 tomorrow morning.

"Last quiz," she said. "The whole thing. No hints."

Raven held the card like a hymnal. "What goes in?"

"Glucose and oxygen. C6H12O6 plus six O2."

"What comes out?"

"Six CO2, six H2O, and energy."

"Where does it happen?"

"The mitochondria, mostly. Powerhouse of the cell, God help me."

"And where does the carbon in your breath come from?"

Alice looked at the card, then at Raven, then out at the water. "The glucose," she said. "It was the glucose all along."

"I have no idea if that's right, but you said it with such confidence," Raven said, crumpling the can. "Come on. If we run, we can get fries before the place closes, and you can respire them for me."

Alice stuffed the cards in her jacket, where they would ride forgotten until laundry day, and ran.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Spike tape is coloured tape used to mark where furniture and actors should be placed on the stage floor.
story:
Ashley had been warned that directing was mostly saying the same sentence in four different tones until one of them worked, and by Wednesday she believed it. The gym smelled of varnish and old basketball, and the drama department had been exiled there for two weeks while the auditorium was refloored. Her one-act, twenty-two minutes of arguments on a sofa, opened in nine days.

The sofa was the problem. It had been donated by somebody's grandmother and it had opinions. Every time Taha and Cyrus carried it onstage for the second scene, it landed somewhere new, and Cyrus, who played the brother who never left the house, kept anchoring his whole performance to wherever he'd set it down. One night his big monologue faced the bleachers. Another night the sofa sat so far downstage that Taha had to deliver her confession to the top of the audience's heads.

"You're blocking yourself," Ashley said, kneeling on the hardwood with her script. "You keep ending up in no one's sightline, including mine."

"The couch moved," Cyrus said. "I swear it moved. I think it wants to leave the play."

Taha stretched out on the offending cushion like a cat in a sunbeam. "It's a method sofa. It's finding its motivation."

Mr. Silva, who taught chemistry and had agreed to keep an eye on the gym in exchange for a folding chair and his newspaper, looked up from the bleachers once during all this. He did not offer advice. He had told Ashley on the first day that directing was her education to ruin, and she suspected he was enjoying the ruination.

She tried discipline first. She measured with her feet, heel to toe, from the stage-left free throw line, and told them the sofa went exactly eleven paces out and four across. For one rehearsal this worked, in the way that a threat works, and then the numbers drifted too, because nobody counted the same way twice and Cyrus rounded down. She tried theology. She tried bribery with vending machine chips. She was starting to habituate herself to failure, greeting it each evening like an annoying neighbour, when Taha, of all people, the one who forgot her lines when the lighting changed, came in from the hardware store with a roll of yellow tape.

"It's spike tape," Taha said, tearing off a strip. "You mark where everything goes. Furniture, actors, whatever."

"You knew this the whole time?"

"I knew it as of forty minutes ago. The cashier told me. She does community theatre and she was very smug about it."

So they taped. An H shape for the sofa's position, neat yellow corners on the floor, and then, because Ashley had gotten carried away, small marks where each actor's feet should land at the top of the scene. Cyrus stepped onto his mark with the relief of a man handed a map after a week in the woods. The sofa, dragged into its taped rectangle, finally sat still, and for the first time the scene looked like a scene instead of an argument happening in a random part of a gym.

Then came the second problem, which was that the actors now behaved like pieces of furniture themselves. They hit their marks and stood there, planted, delivering lines with the fixed cheer of people reciting pithy slogans. The confession that had once wandered the stage now happened entirely from a yellow X, and it was flat, and Ashley sat in the fifth row of folding chairs knowing it was flat and not knowing what to do about it, because the tape had fixed the sofa and somehow broken the people.

She thought about her first approach, the pure freedom of it, everyone moving wherever instinct suggested, which had produced aliveness and total chaos. And she thought about the tape, which produced order and a kind of death. Neither was a direction; they were two wrong answers. So she peeled up some of the smaller marks, the actor ones, and left the sofa's H. "The couch has to be exactly here," she told them, "because Cyrus's whole geography depends on it. But after that, move. Cross when you feel like crossing. If you end up somewhere good, I'll tape it, and then we'll see if it's still good."

"Isn't that backwards?" Cyrus asked. "Tape it after?"

"Tape it after, and argue with it later. That's directing, apparently. You make a decision and then you get to find out if it was one."

They ran it. Taha delivered the confession while crossing away from the sofa, which was not what Ashley had pictured, and it was better than what she had pictured, and she marked the new spot with tape that had not existed as a plan, only as a result. Mr. Silva turned a page. Cyrus did his monologue into the correct section of the audience, then ad-libbed a line about the sofa never going anywhere, and Taha laughed, genuinely, before catching herself.

"We're keeping that," Ashley decided, writing it in the margin, then crossing it out, then writing it again. "Unless we aren't. I'll know Thursday."

"You don't sound sure," Taha said.

"Nine days," said Ashley, and tore off another strip of yellow.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Orthodox or traditionalist historians of the Cold War, writing mainly in the late 1940s and 1950s, blamed its outbreak chiefly on Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe.
story:
Anthony spread the pages across the kitchen table while the dishwasher rattled through its cycle: the textbook open to the chapter on the Cold War's origins, a stack of photocopied documents, and, at the edge of it all, the folded pamphlet from the history museum his class had visited in October. The essay was due in two days, and the prompt Ms. Menon had written on the board was simple enough to be cruel. Weigh two historians' explanations against the evidence, she had said, and tell me what survives.

The pamphlet was what kept pulling at him. He had taken it mostly as a souvenir, a thing to prove he had gone, but that night he actually read the panel text again, and it read like a verdict. The museum's account laid the outbreak of the Cold War at Moscow's door, firmly, without apology. He remembered standing in front of it at fifteen, nodding along, because it was the first story he had been told and it sounded like the shape of the thing. Now the textbook told a different story, one about Western economic power and American ambition, and neither account seemed to know the other existed.

He texted Ann first, then Malakai, and Malakai called back while Anthony was still arranging the documents by country. "My uncle would love that pamphlet," Malakai said, his voice half-muffled, the TV loud behind him. "He's all about the first histories. The orthodox ones, he calls them, the traditionalists. They were writing back in the late forties and early fifties, and they blamed the whole thing chiefly on Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe. That was the story everyone had then." Anthony wrote it down word for word, because it felt like a handle on the pamphlet, a reason it sounded the way it sounded. "But my cousin's professor says that's just the view from the winner's armchair," Malakai added. "So who knows."

Ann came over after dinner, her boots leaving wet prints on the hallway floor, and sat down across from him with her own copy of the documents. She was better at reading against the grain than he was; she underlined the passive verbs, the places where a document made something happen without anyone doing it. "This telegram treats the Soviets like weather," she said. "Like pressure that just moves in." Anthony pulled the textbook back toward himself. "And this one does the same thing to us," he said. "Every American move is a reaction, every Soviet move is a choice." They argued about it for an hour, politely at first, then less politely, until Ann's mother texted and she left with one boot half unlaced, promising to fight about it tomorrow.

Later he tried to suture the two accounts together, laying the orthodox claim beside the textbook's, looking for where they could be stitched and where the fabric simply would not meet. The orthodox story fit some of what he read: the documents did show a Soviet grip tightening on Eastern Europe, and it was hard to read those cables and feel that the fear was invented. But the textbook's story fit other pages, the ones where American officials talked about markets and access and the shape of the postwar world, and those passages made the museum panel look like it had been written with one eye closed.

He took his confusion next door, because Ms. Menon, retired now and growing tomatoes badly in her side yard, had taught history for thirty years and had a habit of answering questions with worse questions. She listened on her porch with her hands around a mug that had gone cold, and when he finished she said only, "So which account explains more of your evidence, and which explains the other account?" He walked home slower than he needed to, turning that second half over. The orthodox historians explained the documents, maybe. The textbook explained the orthodox historians, or thought it did, and that was a different kind of explaining, and he was not sure the essay prompt allowed him to say so.

He wrote until one in the morning, his mother passing through twice to turn off lights he wasn't using. The paragraph that finally came out was less a verdict than a weighing: the orthodox account held where the evidence was about Eastern Europe and lost its footing everywhere the evidence was about money and markets; the textbook was better on the long run and thinner on the first years; both were pernicious in the same quiet way, the way any single-cause story is, by making the other side into a fact of nature. He kept deleting his last sentence because every version sounded more certain than he felt. What stayed uncertain was the part he couldn't document, what any of them had actually intended, and he let the paragraph end there, in the gap, because inventing a bridge would have been easier and false.

Ann read it the next morning in the school parking lot, sitting on the hood of her car with the pages pinned flat against the wind. "You don't pick a side," she said. "Ms. Menon's going to either love this or fail it." Malakai leaned over her shoulder, chewing the last of a granola bar, and pointed at a line near the bottom. "You used the word 'phenomenology' in your notes," he said. "In your notes, not the essay." Anthony took the page back and looked. He had scribbled it two nights before, half asleep, next to a sentence about how each history described a different experience of the same years, the world as each side felt it. He crossed it out, then uncrossed it, and left the note in the margin as it was, one small thing he refused to tidy.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A food bank is usually a central warehouse that collects and distributes food to local agencies, while a food pantry is where people pick up food directly.
story:
The warehouse on Fell Street smelled of cardboard and cold concrete, and Rebecca stood in the loading bay holding a clipboard she did not know how to use. She had signed up because Alicia said it would look good on applications, which Rebecca suspected was a flimsy reason, though she had written it on the form anyway. Mr. Girma, the volunteer coordinator, handed her a box cutter without ceremony and pointed at a pallet of dented cans. "Date check first," he said. "Anything past best-before goes in that bin. Not expired, past best-before. There's a difference, but today there isn't time to argue about it."

She worked next to a boy named Lukas from her chemistry class, whom she knew only as the person who ruined the curve. He sorted quickly and without talking, which she found restful until she didn't. Around ten o'clock she noticed something that began to destabilize her picture of what she was doing here. The parking lot stayed empty. No cars pulled in, no families came through the doors, no one carried out bags of groceries. She had imagined handing a bag of rice to somebody, being thanked, feeling the small satisfying click of usefulness. Instead there was only the warehouse, the pallets, and the hiss of the box cutter tape.

"Where are all the people?" she asked finally. "The hungry people."

Lukas looked up. "What?"

"We've been here two hours and nobody's come in for food. Is it the wrong day?"

Mr. Girma overheard from the office doorway and laughed, not unkindly. "You're waiting for the wrong thing. This is a food bank, not a pantry. A food bank is a central warehouse that collects and distributes food to local agencies. The pantry is where people pick up food directly. We send trucks out to the churches and the schools. Nobody shops here."

Rebecca turned this over while she cut tape. She had used the two words interchangeably her whole life, the way people said dumpster and landfill, and the correction felt simultaneously small and enormous. Somewhere across the city there were pantries, and somewhere at those pantries were the people she had been picturing, and between her and them stood this whole logistics of pallets and agencies and truck routes. Her hour of sorting was not the moment of giving. It was further back in the chain, invisible to whoever received it.

She tested the thought on Alicia at lunch break, in the folding chairs by the coffee urn. Alicia shrugged. "So it still counts for hours. Nobody checks whether you saw an actual poor person."

"That's not what I meant."

"Then what did you mean?"

Rebecca struggled for it. She meant that she had wanted the encounter, the face, and that wanting it felt suddenly like a kind of artifice, a performance she had staged for herself, the volunteer and the grateful stranger, and the warehouse had refused to stage it. But she also meant something else, harder to say: that the pallets were real, that the cans would actually arrive somewhere, and that maybe the chain counted as much as the meeting. She said only, "I thought it would feel more direct." Alicia texted someone for the rest of lunch.

Lukas, when they were back at the pallet, was less dismissive in his own quiet way. "My mom used to go to a pantry," he said, not looking at her. "At the church on Maples. I used to think the food came from the church basement." He stacked a row of tomato paste. "It comes from places like this. From people like us, I guess."

That sentence stayed with her through the afternoon. When Mr. Girma asked for two volunteers to ride along on the afternoon delivery, to the pantry at St. Anselm's, Alicia declined with an excuse about a shift at work, and her refusal was so intransigent that Rebecca stopped asking. She rode in the passenger seat of the van while Lukas navigated from the manifest, and at the church they unloaded crates into a basement room with folding tables and a hand-lettered sign about limits per family.

A woman was already waiting by the door, early, holding a canvas bag folded over her arm. She watched them carry in the boxes without offering to help, and Rebecca watched her watch them, and neither of them spoke. Mr. Girma signed a form on a clipboard at the front desk while the pantry's coordinator counted crates aloud. Rebecca recognized the cans, the exact dented cans she had checked that morning, now stacked on a shelf behind the coordinator's head, and she understood that she still didn't know whether this was the direct thing she had wanted or only another link in it, and that the woman with the canvas bag would not tell her either.

"We open at four," the coordinator said to the woman, gently.

"I know what time you open," the woman said, and sat down on the folding chair closest to the door, and Rebecca went back out to the van for the last crate.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The US federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, though many states and cities set a higher minimum.
story:
Chloe read the notice taped to the camp office window three times before she knocked: JUNIOR COUNSELORS WANTED, PAID, ASK INSIDE. Ms. Tanaka looked up from a tub of name tags and slid a form across the counter, and Chloe filled it out with the same pen she used for everything, the one with the chewed cap, and when she got to the wage line she wrote nothing because the line was blank for her.

"It's seven twenty-five an hour," Ms. Tanaka said. "Same as it's been forever."

Chloe had no idea what that meant. She'd never had money that arrived by the hour, only money that arrived by birthday. She signed anyway, and two weeks later she was leading six seven-year-olds in a game called Sharks and Minnows on the field behind the pavilion, whistle between her teeth, sunburn blooming on her shoulders like a second shirt.

Isabela worked the snack bar in the same camp, and Gurnoor had just started at a day camp one town over, across the state line, so the three of them met on Thursdays at the gas station with the good slushies to compare notes and, eventually, paychecks. Gurnoor unfolded his stub first and laid it flat on the concrete picnic table as though it were a document of some importance, which, to be fair, it was: eleven dollars and change an hour. Isabela's said ten fifty. Chloe's said seven twenty-five, and she laughed when she saw it, a short reflexive laugh, because everyone else was laughing, and then she stopped.

"That can't be right," she said. "We're doing the same job."

"Mine's right," Gurnoor said. "I checked the math twice."

They passed the stubs around like cards, and Chloe felt a small knot of foreboding form under her ribs, the sense that the world had rules she hadn't been told about, and that the rules were older than she was. On her phone, wedged between complaints about the slushie machine, she found it: the federal minimum wage had been seven twenty-five an hour since July 24, 2009. Since before any of them could drive. But many states and cities set a higher minimum, which was why Gurnoor's camp, one state over, paid more, and why Isabela's snack bar fell under the city's rate, and why Chloe's camp sat in the one jurisdiction that hadn't bothered. Nobody had cheated her. Nobody had to. The number transfixed her, the smallness of it and the date, older than her little brother.

"I'm quitting," she announced the next Thursday, before anyone had even sat down. She'd rehearsed it in the car, and it had sounded grandiose there, a declaration of principle, something a person with more courage would say. "It's not fair. Why should I get paid less than you for watching the same kids swim?"

Isabela popped the cap off her slushie and studied the melting blue. "Fair," she said, slowly, like she was weighing the word. Gurnoor started to agree with Chloe, then didn't, then said, "But you like the kids."

That was the trouble. Chloe had spent the morning teaching a boy named Danny to float, and he had held her wrists in the shallow end and kicked until his whole face went from terror to delight, and she had felt, stupidly, like a person who mattered. She wanted to be someone who refused an unfair wage, and she wanted to be the one who caught Danny when he tipped over, and she could not make both wants fit in the same body. The principle was clean and the mornings were not.

On Friday she went to Ms. Tanaka's office, not with a resignation but with the folded phone printout in her fist, sweaty at the creases. Ms. Tanaka read it, set it down, and rubbed her eyes. "I know," she said. "I've known for years. I pay you what the camp pays me to pay you." She looked tired in a way Chloe hadn't let herself notice before. "If you leave, I get somebody who doesn't ask."

Chloe walked back out to the field, where the minnows were already lined up against the fence, Danny among them, waving both arms. She put the whistle back between her teeth. She hadn't decided, exactly; she had decided to decide in August, which felt like a compromise and also like a beginning, and she could not yet tell which. "Ready," she called. "Swim."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Sociologist Ray Oldenburg's 1989 book The Great Good Place named 'third places', such as cafes and libraries, where people meet outside home and work.
story:
The moving truck had left at dawn, and by noon Faith had memorized the back of her mother's head, the way her shoulders crept toward her ears with every lane change. Six hours in the family car. Six hours of the glove compartment, the granola bar wrappers, the phone in her lap showing the last messages from Allie: "this is so unfair" and then, an hour later, "text me when you get there." Josh had not texted at all, which Faith understood to mean something worse than not texting.

"I know you're not talking to me," her mother said, passing a sign for a town with a name Faith refused to learn. "That's allowed. I just want it on the record that it's allowed."

Faith stared out the window at a field of dead sunflowers, all of them facing the same direction, and thought about determinism, which they had covered in Mr. Ahmed's class the week before the move was announced. Every event caused by the event before it. The job offer caused the move, the move caused the six hours in the car, the car caused this silence, and none of it had asked her opinion, which was, she supposed, the whole point of the word.

They arrived in the late afternoon, and the new house smelled like other people's soap. That first night Faith unpacked only her pillow and her charger and lay on the mattress on the floor, introspecting in a way she suspected was not healthy, replaying the lunch table she used to sit at, the exact angle of Allie's laugh, until she fell asleep with her shoes on.

School started Monday. She sat where she was told to sit and answered when spoken to, and by Thursday she understood that the problem was not the school, which was fine, but the after. At her old school, after had meant the diner booth by the window, four of them, fries in the middle. Here, after meant her mother's car, then the house, then the mattress. She tried to introspect her way out of it, decided that was deleterious, and on Friday she did something instead. She asked her mother to drop her at the public library.

"Volunteering?" her mother asked, too bright, hands tightening on the wheel.

"Studying," Faith said, which was technically a plan to sit somewhere that was not the house.

The library had a long table near the periodicals, worn soft at the edges, and she took the end chair. A boy was already there with a battered chess set, playing both sides against himself, and a retired couple argued pleasantly over a crossword two seats down. The next day the boy was there again, and the day after that, and on the fourth day he slid the board an inch toward her without looking up and said, "You play white or you don't play." His name was Marcus. Around them the library did its quiet work: the toddler section erupting and subsiding, the espresso machine in the corner hissing, strangers becoming less strange by proximity.

It was Mr. Ahmed who gave her the word for it, though he did not mean to. Faith had discovered that her old teacher had a sister who worked at this library, and when she came in on a Saturday, there he was at the information desk, wearing a cardigan as if he had never left the classroom. She said hello, braced for pity, and got none. He nodded at the long table, the chess players, the crossword couple, the man who came every day to read the same newspaper from 1989 onward on microfilm. "Third places," he said. "Sociologist Ray Oldenburg, wrote a book about it. The Great Good Place. Home is first, work is second, and these are the third, where people actually meet each other." Then a patron needed him and he was gone, and Faith sat with the phrase all afternoon, turning it over while Marcus sacrificed a bishop to prove a point.

She tested the idea out loud, later, in the car, while her mother navigated the roundabout for the third time. "So like, the diner was a third place. The library here is one. The concept is that you need somewhere that's not home and not work, or you kind of don't meet anyone." Her mother was quiet for a moment, then said, "Your father and I met in a laundromat," in a voice suggesting this was a confession, and Faith laughed for the first time in three weeks.

In October, Allie came to visit, a plan assembled over text with the caution of a treaty. Faith was nervous in a way she hadn't expected, and in the car on the way to the library she rehearsed how she would explain Marcus and the crossword couple, afraid they would sound like a consolation prize. But Allie sat down at the long table, watched Marcus glare at the board, watched the retired woman steal a pen from her husband, and said quietly, "We don't have this. At home we have the diner, but it's just us, always just us, and I never thought about why everything feels so small until right now." She looked almost envious, and Faith, who had spent the whole drive dreading that Allie would see how little she had, realized she had been protecting the wrong person's pride.

That night she texted Josh, who finally wrote back: did you make any friends or is it as bad as you said. She typed the truth, deleted it, typed it again, and sent it anyway. "There's a kid who beats me at chess and a couple who fight over crossword clues and a librarian who quotes sociology at me. It's not the diner." She watched the three dots appear, disappear, appear.

Then her mother called from the hallway, "Faith, your father wants to know if you're coming to the library with us tomorrow, or if you're meeting Marcus there," and through the door she heard her father say, "I'll finally learn how the knight moves," and Faith, still holding the phone, said, "He'll teach you, but he'll make it hurt."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but it acts mainly as a feedback: warmer air holds more water vapor, which amplifies warming started by other gases like carbon dioxide.
story:
The planetarium smelled like dust and projector oil, and Peyton spread her graph across the console table where Mr. Sow let the debate team practice on Thursdays. The graph showed carbon dioxide climbing from a low, wiggling line into a steep, unbroken rise, decade over decade, and she was supposed to be able to explain it to a room full of judges by Saturday.

"Again," said Coby. He was her partner, and he wanted the win more than he wanted dinner, which was why they were here at seven on a school night. "Judges interrupt. I'll be the judge. Go."

She traced the curve with her finger, naming the decades, the steady climb, the way the line seemed to breathe before 1950 and then stop breathing and just go up. Halfway through, Coby held up a hand. "Objection. My source says water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas. So your whole carbon dioxide thing is a sideshow. The real cause is water."

She opened her mouth and nothing came out. The projector hummed above them, throwing a false night sky across the dome, and for a second she just stared at the graph as if it might rearrange itself in her defense. Coby smiled, not unkindly, the way he did when he'd found a hole and intended to drive a truck through it.

"Ask Mr. Sow," she said, but Mr. Sow was in the back rewiring something and had told them twice that he was off the clock for thinking. Kristen, who had come to practice her planetarium volunteer talk and had been sitting in the dark rows taking notes on the stars, called down, "I actually know this one. My talk covers it."

Kristen came down the aisle carrying her own notes, and Peyton felt a small flare of resentment, because Kristen always knew things, and knowing things in front of other people was Kristen's whole project. She wanted the head volunteer spot, the one where you got to run the dome projector yourself, and every fact she collected was another brick in that wall.

"Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas," Kristen said, and Peyton's stomach dropped, because it sounded like Coby was right. "But it acts mainly as a feedback." She tapped Peyton's graph. "Warmer air holds more water vapor, which amplifies warming started by other gases. Like carbon dioxide." She looked at Peyton rather than at Coby, which was either generous or lazy, Peyton couldn't tell. "So say that part yourself. You're the one giving the rebuttal."

Peyton stood under the dome stars and let the pieces settle against each other. The carbon dioxide line climbed first, and the water vapor followed it upward, riding on the warming the way a sound grows in a room with the volume already turned up. The word for it was feedback, and she said it out loud once, quietly, testing the weight of it. Then she turned to Coby and gave the rebuttal twice, the second time faster, and the third time he didn't interrupt at all.

From the back of the dome, Coby watched her run it and felt something between admiration and alarm. He had built his whole cross-examination on the water vapor line, pulled from a website he hadn't checked, and now that line was a wall she could walk through. He could concede it, tonight, honestly, and rebuild his questions around something sturdier. Or he could keep it and gamble that the judges on Saturday knew less than Peyton did. He looked at the graph glowing faintly under the work light, the long relentless rise, and he did not decide yet.

"Ten more minutes," Mr. Sow called from the back, his voice muffled by the panel he was elbow-deep in. "Then I'm killing the lights whether you're geniuses or not."

Peyton rolled the graph and slid it into the tube, and Kristen gathered her notes and started back up the aisle toward the projector booth, where the volunteer coordinator's clipboard hung on a nail by the door. Coby zipped his bag slowly, watching the tube in Peyton's hand like it was evidence.

"So Saturday," he said. "Same objection, or a new one?"

Peyton tucked the tube under her arm. "Try the new one. I'd rather lose to something I haven't heard yet."

He laughed, short, and shouldered his bag. Above them Mr. Sow threw one switch and then another, and the false stars began to wheel.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A 1985 study by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky called basketball's 'hot hand' an illusion, but a 2018 reanalysis by Miller and Sanjurjo found a statistical flaw and evidence of streak shooting.
story:
Olivia found her seat in the second tier just as the anthem finished, wedged between her father and Dan, with Megan two rows down beside the aisle. The stadium's bowl of noise opened around her, forty thousand people already chanting the away player's name, the one the commentators had begun to lionize weeks ago. That player, Koroma, had scored eleven straight points in the semifinal, and half the pregame show had been devoted to whether he was, in the words of one aging pundit, "genuinely on fire."

"He's not on fire," Dan said before Olivia had even unwrapped her scarf. "Nobody's on fire. It's a myth."

"Don't start," Megan called up, turning around in her seat. "You're going to ruin it."

"It's not a myth exactly," Olivia said, and then stopped, because she wasn't sure yet what it was, and she hated saying things she hadn't finished thinking.

The game began in a jagged, contested way, both teams missing early, and Olivia's father offered his usual commentary about effort and heart, words she had grown up inside. He believed in streaks the way he believed in weather signs. When Koroma hit a midrange jumper off a broken play, her father leaned forward. "Here we go," he said, quietly, like a man watching a fire catch.

"Randomness," Dan said. "It's just randomness with a storyline attached." He had done a statistics unit that spring and come out of it evangelical. "There was a study. Nineteen eighty-five. Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky. They looked at the hot hand and said it's an illusion. People see patterns in coin flips."

"Then why does everyone who's ever played swear by it?" Megan said, not turning around this time, which meant she was actually annoyed.

Olivia had read something, hadn't she. Half-read it, on her phone in bed, a paragraph that stuck with her the way certain paragraphs did, without her quite knowing why. She took out her phone now and searched, the screen's glow small against the enormous floodlit field below. Dan noticed and made a dismissive sound, but she kept scrolling. There it was: a 2018 reanalysis by Miller and Sanjurjo. A statistical flaw, the article said, in the original study. And evidence of streak shooting. She read the line twice.

"Okay," she said out loud, and both Dan and her father looked at her, and Megan turned around, and the game went on unregarded for a moment, a fast break happening below them like weather. "There was a study in 1985, Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky, and they said the hot hand is an illusion. That's real. But in 2018, Miller and Sanjurjo reanalyzed it, and they found a statistical flaw, and evidence of streak shooting."

"A flaw," her father repeated, tasting the word.

"So the hot hand is real," Megan said.

"So I was right," Dan said, at almost the same moment, and then they both frowned at each other.

"No," Olivia said. "That's what I keep doing, though. Picking a side fast because it's easier to hold than a maybe." Koroma missed a three, badly, air ball, and a groan moved through the bowl like wind through wheat. "The first study was wrong and the second one might be righter, but one reanalysis isn't the whole truth either. It's more like the truth is expensive and we keep getting partial refunds."

Dan laughed at that, which surprised her, because she had meant it seriously. "Partial refunds," he said. "That's grim."

"It's honest," she said. She was thinking of her own decisions lately, the college deposits, the way she had circled one option and crossed it out and circled it again, as though momentum itself were evidence. Her father was the opposite: he committed and never looked back, and called the looking back weakness. Somewhere between his certainty and Dan's dismissal was a position she could actually stand on, and she could feel herself assembling it in real time, in a plastic seat, under lights.

Koroma scored twice more in the third quarter, and the crowd's noise changed pitch, became a held breath rather than a shout. "He's on fire," Megan said, and it wasn't an argument now, it was a kind of hope.

"Maybe," Dan said, and it cost him something to say it.

Olivia watched the player run back on defense, his face blank, no way to read from outside what was happening inside. "Maybe," she agreed. The horn sounded for the timeout and the noise rolled up over them, and she put her phone away and leaned forward into it.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: The Soviet Union refused Marshall Plan aid and pressed Eastern European governments, including Czechoslovakia, to withdraw after first showing interest.
story:
The city archive smelled of warm dust and old glue, and Maelie had claimed the same table in the corner for three Saturdays running. She spread out her two books like rival witnesses. The first, by a historian named Horn, argued that the United States had used economic aid to aggrandize itself in Europe, turning generosity into leverage until the continent split in two. The second, by a woman named Ostrova, held that the split was already made, that the Soviets would accept no plan that required opening their sphere to Western money, and that the Americans had offered in good faith. Maelie's essay was due Tuesday, and Ms. Ferreira had written one line on her draft: "Pick one. Then tell me what it costs you."

The problem was that she couldn't pick one, and she wasn't sure Ms. Ferreira meant that as permission.

Mila slid into the chair across from her, dropping a vending machine coffee on the table hard enough to slop it over the rim. "You're still on that? We handed our drafts in a week ago."

"Mine came back." Maelie turned the draft so Mila could see the red line. "She wants a considered position. I have two positions and a headache."

"Then flip a coin." Mila peeled the lid off her cup. "That's what London did for the causes of the war essay last year and she got a B plus."

"London's a raconteur, not an historian. She once told the whole class her family was descended from Hungarian nobility, and her mom's from Peckham."

Mila laughed, then lowered her voice because a man at the microfilm reader, a garrulous retiree who had spent an hour narrating every frame to nobody, glanced over. Maelie pulled the printout toward her. It was a reproduction from the archive's Cold War exhibition downstairs, a map of Europe with the countries that accepted the plan shaded green, and the East blank as an unwritten page. She had copied it because something about it snagged her.

"Here's what I keep circling," she said. "Horn says the Americans designed the plan so the Soviets would refuse it. Ostrova says the Soviets refused it because they were determined to control Eastern Europe no matter what. Both of them use this map. Both of them look at the same blank space."

Mila squinted at it. "So which one's lying?"

"Neither, maybe. That's the worst part."

She had gone down to the exhibition that first Saturday mainly to escape the reading room, and there she had found the thing neither historian had printed in full: a display case with a quotation from the Czechoslovak government. It was dated to the spring of the plan, and it expressed interest, real interest, in the aid. Maelie had stood in front of the case for a long time, because both her historians had told her the Eastern governments never wanted it, that refusal was a foregone conclusion. The map said the East withdrew. The case said the East had first leaned in.

She told Mila this now, and Mila, who had a way of asking the blunt question Maelie was avoiding, said, "So who made them withdraw?"

"The display doesn't say." Maelie tapped the map. "It just shows the blank countries. The card underneath says the Soviet Union refused the aid itself, and pressed the Eastern governments to withdraw too, Czechoslovakia included, after they'd shown interest. That's all it gives you. No why."

"And you can't write 'no why' in an essay."

"No." Maelie sat back. "But listen. Horn needs the refusal to be America's doing, a trap. If Czechoslovakia wanted in first, then someone else closed the door. Ostrova needs the refusal to be the Soviets' choice, freely made. But if they had to press the governments, lean on them, then the choice wasn't clean on that side either. It's like both of them sanded the edges off the same fact."

"So which side does the fact favor?"

Maelie looked at the map again. "Ostrova's, partly. The pressure came from the Soviet side; that's in the record. But it doesn't prove the Americans offered innocently. It just doesn't disprove it." She heard how weak that sounded and pressed on anyway. "I think the honest position is: the evidence supports the Soviet refusal as deliberate, and leaves the American motive in the dark. And I think that's what Ms. Ferreira meant by the cost."

Mila drank her coffee and watched her. "You're going to hand in an essay that says 'probably this, unknowably that.' You know that's what you're doing."

"Yes."

"You're braver than me."

The retiree at the microfilm machine had gone quiet at last. Outside the tall windows, the November light was thinning over the rooftops, and the reading room lamps came on one by one down the rows, small yellow pools in the grey. Maelie pulled the draft back toward herself and crossed out her old opening paragraph with two slow strokes. Underneath it she wrote: "Both historians treat Czechoslovakia's withdrawal as settled. The archive treats it as an event." She looked at the sentence for a moment, then closed the notebook.

Mila stood, gathering her cup. "Text me if Ferreira destroys you."

"She won't." Maelie zipped her bag around the books, both of them, still rivals, still in her bag. "I'll let her destroy one half and see which one survives."

She carried the map printout downstairs to return it to the exhibition desk, and on the way she passed the display case with the Czechoslovak quotation, the glass reflecting her own face over the faded type, and she stopped, and read it once more, all the way to the end.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that moving from casual friend to friend takes about 90 hours together.
story:
The truck was louder than Eva expected, a hollow drumming that made every sentence an act of leaning close and shouting, which suited her fine because she didn't want to talk anyway. Mr. Abdi, the neighbour who had offered to drive the rented truck because, he said, he liked an excuse to see the highway, let her ride up front with the last boxes. Her mother followed behind in the Honda with the plants and the dog. By sundown they had to turn the truck in at the rental office in the new town, and Eva had exactly that long to decide what to do about the folded piece of paper in her jacket pocket.

The paper was from Mr. Abdi, actually, handed over at the curb that morning while her mother was taping the last box. He'd torn it from a magazine in the cab, some article about friendship he'd half-read at a dentist's office two years ago and never forgotten. "Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study," Lilly had read aloud from it on the phone last night, snorting. "Estimated that moving from casual friend to friend takes about ninety hours together. Ninety, Eva. You and me did that in like two months of lunches."

"It took us one summer of the pool," Eva had said, and Lilly had said, "Right, because we cheated," and then neither of them had said anything for a second, because the pool was in the old town and the new town had a river nobody swam in.

Now the highway unspooled and Mr. Abdi drove with his elbows high on the wheel, and Eva held the paper and did the arithmetic she'd been doing for two days. Ninety hours. School started Monday. If she joined even one club, some club, any club, she'd see the same faces every week, and the hours would accumulate whether the club was good or not. Chess. Environmental committee. It didn't matter. The math was indifferent to the club, which felt both comforting and slightly grim, like being told friendship was a shift you could clock into. "You're quiet," Mr. Abdi said. "Sign's saying gas in fourteen miles. Want anything?"

"Tea," she said, and then, because the drumming made confessions easier, "Can I ask you something dumb?"

"Those are the only ones I answer."

"If you had to start over somewhere, knowing nobody. Would you do it on purpose? Like, schedule it?"

He was quiet long enough that she thought she'd offended him. "When I came to this country," he said, "I knew the exact hour. I'd count weeks at my job like a man counting debts." He glanced at her. "But I'll tell you a flaw in your schedule. Ninety hours can pass with someone and you still don't know them, if you spend all ninety pretending to be easy to like. I did that for a year. It was a very ascetic year, actually. Very disciplined. Very lonely."

The detraction, if there was one, wasn't the number. The number was probably fine, she thought as the gas station swelled up out of the fields. It was what she'd been planning to do with it: pick a club, manufacture hours, extenuate the whole awkwardness of being new by calling it arithmetic. Lilly would never do that. Lilly had made friends by falling off a dock.

In the parking lot, phone held up to the one bar of signal under the awning, she called. Shift, now, to the other end of the line: Lilly, sitting on her kitchen floor with the freezer open against her ankles, bracing to say something and then robbed of the chance when Eva spoke first.

"There's a robotics club," Eva said, "Tuesday and Thursday, plus Saturday practices, which is like eleven hours a week before you count lunches. Hall's study says ninety hours, so basically eight weeks and I'd have friends, that's the whole plan, I have a plan, Lilly."

"Your plan has one detractor," Lilly said, aiming for funny and landing somewhere near it. "You."

"Okay but that's why I'm calling you."

"You're calling me so I'll say don't be somebody you're not, join the thing you'd actually want even if nobody hot is in it."

"No," Eva said, and then, "partly no. I'm calling because the ninety hours thing goes both ways and we already paid ours, so you're not allowed to just be my old friend. You have to be my current one. That's a different job and I'm assigning it to you."

Lilly laughed, one syllable, the kind that catches on something. "Fine. But if you join chess club out of desperation I'm never visiting."

The Honda pulled in beside the truck, her mother waving through the windshield, and Eva looked at the clock on the dash through the glass: forty minutes to the rental deadline, three days until the new school, eight weeks, by one study, until friend. Mr. Abdi was already at the register buying his own tea without asking what she wanted, which was either rude or a kind of trust. She pressed the phone harder to her ear.

"Tuesday," she said. "I'll sign up Tuesday. Now tell me about the dock again, the whole thing, from the beginning."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: A launch velocity v at an angle θ above the horizontal splits into a horizontal component v cos θ and a vertical component v sin θ.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and hot extension cords, and Alexa's launcher stood on the folding table between a volcano that had already erupted twice and a display about sedimentary rock layers cut from cardboard. Her project was a compressed-air cannon that fired a marble at a fixed speed, with a protractor bolted to the pivot so the launch angle could be set to the degree. The object was to predict where the marble would land, mark the spot with a paper cup, and let the marble prove the math right.

At rehearsal the night before, it had proved the math wrong. Every time. At forty-five degrees the marble sailed past the cup by half a metre, and at twenty degrees it fell short. Alexa had stayed up until one in the morning, checking the arithmetic over and over, until her mother had come down the hall in her robe and turned off the desk lamp.

Now Taylor arrived first, carrying the sign they had painted together, and behind Taylor came Rory, who was not in their physics class but had come, he claimed, for the free juice boxes in the cafeteria. Rory leaned over the prediction sheet, a table of angles with their computed ranges in Alexa's careful handwriting, and tapped the twenty-degree row.

"You're saying if we shoot it almost flat, it goes two metres," Rory said. "And at seventy degrees it also goes two metres. So they go the same distance."

"That's what the formula gives," Alexa said. "The range comes out the same for an angle and its complement. That part is right. The whole thing is off by some other amount."

Taylor had done the component work. Alexa had handled the timing, and together they had split the launch velocity into two pieces without arguing about it, because it had seemed obvious at the time. Taylor had taken the vertical component and Alexa the horizontal, and they had each written down a trig ratio and handed them across the table like exchanging cards. Neither of them had checked the other's.

Ms. Wiśniewski came by at ten, holding a clipboard and a cup of coffee that had clearly gone cold some time ago. She fired the launcher once at thirty degrees, watched the marble thump down beyond the cup, and made a small mark on her sheet. "Run it again when you've got it sorted," she said, and moved on to the volcano.

Alexa stood looking at the protractor. She set the angle to eighty-five degrees, nearly straight up, and stared at it while Taylor read out their numbers. Then she took the pencil and drew a triangle on the back of the prediction sheet, a long thin triangle, the launch velocity as its slanted side, the angle at the bottom marked twenty degrees.

"Taylor," she said, "when the angle is small, almost flat, how much of the velocity should be pointing up?"

"A tiny bit," Taylor said. "Almost none."

"And what did we put in for the vertical part?"

Taylor looked at the sheet. The vertical column said the full velocity times the cosine of twenty degrees, which was nearly the whole velocity. Taylor's face changed slowly, the way a person's face changes when they reread a sentence they have read fifty times and finally see what it says.

"I swapped them," Taylor said. "I did sine for the horizontal and cosine for the vertical."

At eighty-five degrees the mistake was enormous: their sheet claimed a nearly vertical launch would send the marble almost straight out sideways, and a flat launch would send it almost straight up. Alexa felt the whole term of confusion rearrange itself, like the cardboard rock layers finding their true order, oldest at the bottom. A launch velocity at an angle splits, she thought, into a horizontal component, the velocity times the cosine, and a vertical component, the velocity times the sine, and Taylor had simply crossed the wires.

They redid the table in twenty minutes, Taylor calling out ratios, Alexa doing the squares. Rory tried to cajole them into a victory launch before the judges returned, but Alexa made him wait while she checked the horizontal column twice, because she could no longer assume the obvious parts were safe.

Ms. Wiśniewski came back at eleven with her clipboard. Alexa set the angle to thirty degrees, placed the cup where the new number said, and pressed the valve. The marble rose, hung for a moment in the reverie of its arc, and dropped into the cup with a sound like a coin in a dish.

"Run it at sixty," Ms. Wiśniewski said. "Show me the other one."

Alexa rotated the protractor, did the arithmetic aloud, and moved the cup to the new mark, the same mark, two metres out. Rory folded his arms. Taylor held the valve.

"Fire," Alexa said.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The Suzuki method, developed by Japanese violinist Shinichi Suzuki, teaches children to play by ear before reading music, the way they learn to speak before reading.
story:
The band room smelled of cork grease and the ghost of thirty years of concerts, and Jordyn sat in the back corner with the rented trumpet the school had assigned her in September, three months and one embo-chure disaster after she'd signed up for band as a senior. She could read the music fine. That was the strange part. She'd taken piano at seven and theory at twelve, and the notation on the stand was as legible to her as a grocery list. What she could not do was make the sounds in her head come out of the horn. Ms. Hamdan had said, kindly, that she played like someone translating from a dictionary, one word at a time.

The kid across the room was making it look easy. He was maybe nine, a neighbor's son who came in on Tuesdays for a lesson before the high schoolers arrived, and he played a whole melody on his small violin without any paper in front of him at all. Jordyn watched him finish the tune and lower the instrument, and she asked how he'd memorized it, assuming he'd worked it out from a score.

"I didn't memorize it," he said. "My teacher plays it and I copy it. I can't read notes yet."

Jordyn looked at the empty stand in front of him, then at her own crowded one. "You're kidding. How long have you played?"

"Two years. My mom calls it the Suzuki method. After Shinichi Suzuki. He was a violinist from Japan."

She'd never heard of it. The name meant nothing to her, which bothered her more than it should have, since she'd assumed her years of theory were the only real way in. She tried to imagine a kid speaking fluent sentences before knowing the alphabet, and then, immediately afterward, a kid playing fluent music before knowing a note was middle C. The two images refused to sit apart from each other.

When Jaden came in for the Wednesday rehearsal, he found her still thinking about it. Jaden wanted the first trumpet part in the winter concert, wanted it enough that he'd been practicing the Haydn-ish arrangement since October, and he was not generous about competition. "Why are you staring at that little kid's stand?" he said, dropping his case on the table with a belligerent little bang, daring her, she supposed, to have opinions about territory.

"He plays by ear," she said. "He can't read a note. He plays by ear the way kids talk before they learn to read." She heard herself equivocate as soon as she said it, softening the claim in case she had it wrong, hedging where she had no reason to hedge. "I read everything and I can't play anything. That's the actual situation."

"Then practice more," Jaden said, which was the answer of an egoist who believed that whatever he had, he had earned, and whatever anyone lacked, they lacked by character. He snapped his case open and began his warm-up arpeggios at a volume meant to end the conversation.

Jordyn closed her book of exercises. She set the stand's pages face down on the table. Then she lifted the trumpet and, slowly, badly, with two false starts and a cracked high note that made Dante in the percussion section glance over, she tried to play back the melody the kid had played, the one that was still hanging around in her memory like a phrase of overheard speech. She got the first four bars. She got the next four wrong, found the note under the right one, corrected, went on. It was not good. It was, for the first time, hers.

Ms. Hamdan came out of her office with a stack of folders and stopped in the doorway, listening without saying anything, which Jordyn appreciated more than any compliment. When she finished the phrase, the room held still for a second.

"Again," said Ms. Hamdan, "without the paper."

Jordyn wiped her mouth on her sleeve, put her fingers back on the valves, and started the tune over from the first note.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Integrating a velocity function over a time interval gives the displacement, which is the area under the velocity-time graph.
story:
The quiz on integrals was on Friday, and by Wednesday Clara still could not make the symbols mean anything. She could follow the notation, could even reproduce the little stretched S in her notebook until it looked like a signature, but the leap from antiderivative to area under a curve had the quality of a card trick. She kept waiting for the reveal, and it kept not arriving.

Ms. Hernández had said, at the end of Tuesday's lesson, that anyone who wanted extra help could come to room 114 at lunch. Clara had not gone. She suspected, correctly, that Ms. Hernández's help would consist of the same explanation delivered more slowly, and what Clara wanted was not slowness. She wanted the thing itself, whatever it was, to stop hiding.

Thursday morning her grandfather drove her to the dentist because her mother had a shift. The appointment was in Twenty Mile River, which was, according to the sign outside town, twenty miles away. Clara, staring out the window with her math book open on her knees in a gesture that fooled no one, glanced at the speedometer instead. Forty. She wrote it on the back of a receipt. A minute later, forty-five. Then fifty-two, because her grandfather drove the way he talked, steadily, with bursts of emphasis.

"Are you timing me?" he asked, without turning his head.

"Sort of. I'm reading the speedometer every minute."

"For a class?"

"For me." This was true, though she had not known it was true until she said it. She kept going. Forty-eight for a while, then fifty, then the long crawl of road construction where they held at fifteen, and Clara wrote the numbers down in a column, feeling faintly ridiculous, and then not ridiculous at all.

The dentist found nothing to drill, which made her grandfather effusive; he praised the hygienist, the parking situation, the winter light on the river, the entire scam-proof integrity of the town of Twenty Mile River. On the drive back Clara did not record anything. She was thinking about her column of numbers, and about the odometer, which had advanced by slightly more than forty miles round trip, a fact she had checked at the parking lot while her grandfather hunted for his keys.

That evening she sat at the kitchen table with graph paper and drew it out. Speed on the vertical axis, time on the horizontal, one minute per square. The points made a jagged line, and she connected them. Then she sat with her pencil hovering, because she remembered the odometer. The odometer did not care about speed at any single instant; it accumulated. So she tried something. If the car had held at exactly forty miles per hour for one whole minute, it would have covered forty-sixtieths of a mile in that minute. She did that for each number in the column and added them up. Twenty point something. She checked it against the road sign, twenty miles, and against the odometer, and sat very still for a moment, the way a person does when a door they had been leaning on swings open.

She was reaching for her phone to text Avneet when she noticed the rectangle problem. Each minute's block was a rectangle, width one minute, height the speed. The area of each rectangle was the distance for that minute. The total area was the total distance. The jagged graph she had drawn was the velocity over time, and the area underneath it, the actual literal shaded area, was how far they had gone. It had been sitting there the whole time on the graph paper, ordinary, flat, blue ink, and she had walked past it for two weeks.

On Friday morning she found Avneet at the lockers and showed her the graph paper, the column of speeds, the rectangles. Avneet was loud in her approval, as she was loud in everything, and leaned in so that her backpack swung against Clara's hip. "Wait, so the area under your graph is twenty miles? That's the whole trip?"

"It's called displacement," Clara said. "The integral of velocity over the time interval gives the displacement, which is the area under the velocity-time graph." She heard Ms. Hernández's phrasing come out of her own mouth, word for word, and wondered when exactly she had memorized it, since it had clearly not been on Friday that she understood it. Somewhere between the two, the sentence had been waiting in her like a key in a pocket.

Curtis materialized at the mention of the quiz, because Curtis had a talent for arriving whenever anyone said the word quiz. "You're explaining it to her," he said, in the tone of a man discovering an injustice. "Explain it to me. I've been trying to codify this stuff all week, I have notes, I have a system." His system, Clara had seen it, was a page of formulas boxed and starred with no connective tissue whatsoever, a filing cabinet with nothing in the drawers.

"It's not a formula," Clara said. "Well, it is, but that's not what it is." She was aware that this sounded unhelpful, and that she could not immediately do better. She took out the graph paper again. "Look. Speedometer, every minute." She walked him through the rectangles, one at a time, and watched his face do the thing hers had probably done at the kitchen table, disbelief, then arithmetic, then the quiet settling.

In class Ms. Hernández put the first problem on the board, a velocity function and a time interval, and asked for the displacement. Clara drew the curve, shaded under it lightly, and began. She was honest with herself about the edges of what she knew: her grandfather had gone varying speeds within each minute, and her rectangles had smoothed that over, and she did not yet know how the notation fixed it, or whether it fixed it perfectly. That part stayed dark. But the area itself, the shaded blue strip under a curve, had told the truth once, and she was willing to follow it again. Beside her, Curtis was drawing rectangles, muttering, his system abandoned at the edge of the desk.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: The United States has no national sales tax; sales taxes are set by states and local governments, so the rate on a receipt depends on where the purchase is made.
story:
Michael counted the bills twice before he reached the teller window, because the number on his paycheque and the number in his hand were not the same number, and he wanted to be sure he knew which one was real. The cheque said 512 dollars. The envelope from his shift manager at the garden centre said 431 dollars and change. He had worked ninety-one hours over three weeks, hauling mulch and ringing up fertilizer, and somewhere between those hours and this envelope, eighty dollars had gone somewhere without asking him.

"That's income tax and payroll deductions," said Mr. Rodríguez from the desk beside the tellers, without looking up from his paperwork. He was the branch officer who had opened Michael's account in June, a man with reading glasses pushed low and a habit of saying only what he had evidence for. "You'll see it all itemized on the stub. You can file a return in the spring and maybe get some of it back, depending."

Michael slid the cheque under the glass and studied the stub while the teller keyed in the deposit. Federal income tax. State income tax. FICA, which he did not recognize and which took the largest single bite. He had assumed, in the vague way he assumed things about adulthood, that a wage was a wage, and that money you earned arrived whole, like a mark on a report card. Instead it arrived like a photograph of itself, slightly reduced, edges cropped by people he would never meet.

He was saving for a car, an ugly and reliable one, because in September he would be driving himself to the state college two hours away, and his mother's schedule at the hospital did not include him. The account balance after today read 1,906 dollars. The car he wanted was 2,400. He had done the arithmetic so many times that the gap between the numbers felt like a family trait, something in his lineage: grandmother's pension letter tacked to her fridge, his mother reading her own pay stub at the kitchen table with her lips moving.

In August, Gwyneth asked him to drive her to the college's open house, and they took his mother's car and split the gas. Gwyneth was going to study economics, which she announced the way other people announced allergies, as a fact about herself that others would have to accommodate. Halfway there they crossed the state line, a green sign and a sudden change in how the road felt under the tires, and stopped at a gas station in a town whose name Michael forgot immediately. He bought the same bag of chips and the same bottle of root beer he had bought the week before at home, and the total was different. Not the prices. The total.

"Tax," the cashier said, when he asked, in the tone of a person reporting weather.

Gwyneth leaned over the counter and looked at the receipt, and then at his older receipt, which he still had folded in his wallet because he was keeping every receipt that summer, tallying them against his account. "We don't have a national sales tax," she said. "It's the states and the local governments that set it, so the rate on a receipt depends on where you buy the thing." She said it flatly, handing both receipts back, and Michael stood in the fluorescent doorway holding them side by side, two small grey documents describing the same chips at two different totals, thirty cents apart, and the reason was simply where his feet had been standing.

At the open house, a financial aid officer described a scholarship as munificent, beaming, and Michael imputed to her a sincerity he could not verify, the way he had once imputed honesty to a government that took FICA from a seventeen-year-old's mulch money. He sat in the back row and did the math on the folder in front of him: deductions on one side, a refund possibly coming in spring, sales tax leaking out of him county by county, scholarship money that was real and also not money in his hand. He could hold both ideas now, that the numbers would take their share no matter what, and that the share depended on the ground under him, and he could choose some of that ground. He did not know yet how much choosing mattered. He wrote 2,400 on the folder, then crossed it out and wrote 2,167, which was the balance minus the gas and the chips.

On the drive home, Gwyneth slept with her cheek against the window, and Michael crossed back over the state line in the dark, and when he stopped for gas he stood at the pump a moment before going in, reading the town's name on the sign, because it turned out that mattered too.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In the UK, students apply to university through UCAS and can choose up to five courses, listed in no order of preference.
story:
The cursor blinked in the box marked "Course choices" and Victor had been watching it for a long time, as if it might blink first. On the screen behind it, six tabs were open, one for each university he wanted, and the trouble was arithmetic: six did not fit into five.

"You're still on that?" His mother set a mug of tea on the desk, far from the keyboard, the way he liked. "You've been at it since supper."

"UCAS," he said. "You apply through this one place, and you get five courses. Five, total. And it doesn't even rank them. You just list five, in no order of preference, and they all weigh you the same."

"So pick five."

"It's not picking. It's cutting." He scrolled his list so she could see the sixth, the one at Edinburgh, ancient and grey in the photographs, the one he had wanted since he was fourteen and had seen a documentary about its observatory. "Everything about this one feels right and I can't say why, and everything about the London one makes sense on paper and I can't make myself cross out either."

She touched his shoulder and left him to it, which was its own kind of help.

He texted Zakk, who replied in his usual fragments. "just pick the best 5." Victor typed back that there was no best, that was the whole problem, there was only different. Zakk sent a shrugging emoji and then, a minute later, "come to the shop. sylvia's here."

The shop was Zakk's father's hardware store, and Sylvia was sitting on a stack of paint tins eating crisps while Zakk alphabetised screws nobody would ever buy. Victor laid out the problem the way he had come to think of it: two selves, one choosing. "There's the one who wants the place with the observatory and the cold winters and the town that closes at nine. And there's the one who wants London, because London is where things happen, where I'd actually meet the people doing the work I want to do."

"Antiquated," said Sylvia, gesturing at the shelf of brass hinges behind her, "like these. Zakk's dad won't sell them online. He says the shop is the shop." She brushed salt from her fingers. "Maybe the question isn't which self is real. Maybe you get to pick which one you feed."

"That's very wise," Victor said, "from someone eating crisps on paint."

"I contain multitudes."

He walked home the long way, past Mr. Menon's house, where the porch light was always on because Mr. Menon read late and didn't mind who knew it. The old man was out front with a blanket over his knees, and when Victor explained the five-course problem, listing the universities like a litany, Mr. Menon listened all the way through, which most adults did not.

"Cut the one that hurts least," Mr. Menon said finally.

"That's the advice? Cut the one that hurts least?"

"No. Think about why it hurts least. That tells you something." He pulled the blanket higher. "And don't hand me a peroration about destiny. At your age I gave a speech to my father about my calling. He fell asleep before the end of it, and he was right to."

Victor laughed, and said goodnight, and walked the last two blocks saying nothing at all.

At his desk he opened the six tabs again and read them, one at a time, slowly. The London course he could defend line by line: modules, lecturers, a placement year. The Edinburgh one he could only defend the way you defend a song you love, badly, by playing it. Then there was Manchester, solid and unglamorous, the course he had added because his uncle lived there and it would be free housing. He examined his own reluctance and found it wasn't about the city. It was that he had chosen it for comfort, and comfort, he realised, was the version of himself he least wanted to feed.

Zakk texted: "well?" and Victor typed "dropping Manchester" and then, before he could demur with himself, before the thought could finish forming that maybe free housing was wisdom and not cowardice, he clicked the remove button anyway. Four remained, and the fifth slot sat empty, and he knew Edinburgh and London would have to fight it out for it, and he did not yet know who won.

His mother appeared in the doorway with the empty mug. "Decided?"

"One out," he said. "Five minus one to go."

"Tea?" she asked, holding up the mug.

"Yes, please," said Victor, and turned back to the screen.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: The Hindu festival of Holi falls on the full moon of the month Phalguna, usually in March, and begins with a bonfire the night before called Holika Dahan.
story:
The parking lot behind the community hall smelled of smoke and fried dough, and Riley stood at the edge of it holding a paper plate he had no intention of eating from. His aunt had pressed it into his hands at the door with the words "You're too thin, you look like a photo of yourself," and then disappeared into the crowd of relatives whose names he was supposed to remember and mostly didn't. His mother was somewhere inside; his father had stayed home with a cold that Riley suspected was diplomatic rather than viral.

He had come for a reason, though, and the reason was standing across the lot by the woodpile, wearing a denim jacket over her kurta. Mahi had texted him three times that afternoon. Are you going. You should go. I'll meet you there. She was in his sociology class, the one person at school who knew what Holi was without him having to explain it, and tomorrow morning, at the park, the colors were supposed to start at ten. He had promised to bring the old white shirt his mother kept for exactly this purpose, folded in a drawer like evidence.

"I thought the colors were tonight," he said, coming up beside her. His hands were in his pockets. The plate hovered awkwardly at his side.

"Tonight's the fire," Mahi said. She nodded toward the pile of logs and old branches that the uncles had been stacking since sundown, arguing the whole time about the arrangement the way they argued about everything, with great volume and no malice. "Tomorrow is the colors."

This was the gap in his knowledge that he had been hoping no one would find. His parents had split the calendar between them when he was seven, his mother keeping the festivals, his father keeping the summers, and Riley had grown up attending Holi the way one attends a language class twice a year: functional, halting, always slightly behind. He knew the colors. He knew the sweets. He did not know why a bonfire came first, or when, or what it was called.

An uncle, the loud one from the woodpile arguments, spotted him and waved him over with a big insouciant gesture, as though Riley had been hiding and had now been caught. "Come, come. You will help or you will watch. Watching is also a job."

Riley set his plate on a folding table and went. The fire had not been lit. The uncles were consulting a phone, which struck Riley as funny until he heard what they were consulting it for.

"The full moon," the loud uncle was saying to another man. "It has to be the full moon of Phalguna. That is the rule. Usually March, this time of year, and tonight is that night. The fire is tonight and the colors are tomorrow."

"Then light it," the other man said.

"In a minute. The moon is full but the aunties are still eating."

Riley drifted back toward Mahi, turning this over. So the festival had a clock in the sky. It moved with the moon, not with a printed date, which explained why his mother's reminders arrived at seemingly random times in late winter. He felt the small satisfaction of a mechanism understood, and beneath it, something less tidy: the realization that he had been treating a whole system as a single day when it was actually two, a night and a morning, each with its own name.

"What's the fire called?" he asked Mahi. "It has a name, doesn't it."

"Holika Dahan," she said, easy as anything, watching the woodpile. "Tonight is Holika Dahan."

He said the words back to himself. Holika Dahan. Tomorrow, colors. He could feel the shape of it now, a beginning and then a release, though what the bonfire itself meant, what story it carried, he still could not have said. That part stayed dark, the way the lot stayed dark before the match.

The uncles lit the fire at last, and it went up faster than anyone expected, a column of orange that made the whole crowd step backward at once. Somebody's phone played music. Somebody's small cousin screamed with delight and then, seconds later, with fear. Riley stood beside Mahi in the heat, and his mother appeared at his other shoulder holding two cups of chai, pressing one into his hand without a word.

"Tomorrow, ten o'clock," Mahi said. "White shirt."

"Ten o'clock," he said.

The flames caught a branch that had been added carelessly, and it fell with a soft thud back onto the pile, sending a spray of sparks up past the moon.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Tennessee Williams called The Glass Menagerie, first staged in Chicago in 1944, a memory play: it is narrated by Tom, who looks back on his family.
story:
The assignment sheet said ten minutes, one moment from your own life, and Olivier had spent three evenings failing to make the night his father left into anything that worked on a stage. He sat in the empty drama room after fifth period, the chairs pushed back against the wall, and read the same stage directions over and over. In his draft, a boy packed a suitcase while a woman cried in the kitchen, and it was accurate and completely dead.

Rocco came in with a bag of chips and dropped into the seat beside him. "Mr. Torres says yours is the only one he hasn't gotten yet," he said, crumpling the bag. "That's either a compliment or a death sentence."

"It's all just people standing around being sad," Olivier said. "I know how it felt. I don't know how it looked."

"Ask me, I was there," Rocco said. Rocco had been fourteen and eating cereal at the kitchen table when the door closed. The school had lionized nothing about that night; nobody had, which was part of the problem. In Olivier's memory the whole event had no audience, no shape, just a hallway and a sound.
