That night he searched the shelf in his mother's room, the one she called her college books, and found a thin paperback with a glass unicorn on the cover. He'd grabbed it mostly because it was short. But the opening pages weren't a scene at all. A man stood outside the action and talked straight out, and Olivier sat on the edge of her bed and read the whole introduction twice. At school the next morning he found Mr. Torres before first bell. "Tennessee Williams called The Glass Menagerie a memory play," Olivier said. "First staged in Chicago, 1944. Tom narrates it, looking back on his family."

"That's the one," Mr. Torres said. He didn't add anything, just held the door. He had a way of letting a discovery sit there without decorating it.

So Olivier gave his play a narrator. He wrote a boy at the side of the stage, older than the scene, speaking to the audience while the kitchen went on without him. It fixed the deadness immediately, but it created a second problem, and he saw it at the read-through on Thursday. With the narrator standing outside, the mother in the scene became thinner, more pitiful, a prop for the boy's grief. His own mother, he had to admit, had been obstreperous that night, furious, not weeping, throwing a shoe at the door after it had already closed. He had written her crying because it was easier to narrate. He went home and rewrote her, and the narrator's speeches got shorter and more doubtful, and the play got better and harder.

Rocco read the new draft and frowned at one page. "This leitmotif thing, the door sound three times. Is that a real technique or did you make it up?"

"It's from music. It's a thing that comes back." Olivier pointed at the page. "The latch, the kettle, the latch. She hears the door before he's even gone."

"That's actually creepy," Rocco said, which from Rocco was a review.

Dennis, who was directing, staged the narrator at the edge of the lighting, half in the dark. They ran it in the drama room on a Tuesday after school, chairs dragged into two rough rows, and Olivier watched his own life from the back of the room with his arms crossed so nobody could see his hands. The kettle screamed. The latch clicked twice. The mother threw the shoe and then stood with her back to everyone, and the narrator said, "I have told this the same way for three years, and I don't think it happened this way," and the audience, eleven people, went quiet in a way Olivier could feel on his skin.

Afterward Mr. Torres collected the chairs and said only, "Thursday, full run, be off book." In the parking lot Rocco caught up with him. "My mom wants to come," he said. "I told her it was about your dad. She said she'd still like to come."

Olivier stopped beside the bike rack. He hadn't thought about the mother in the audience, the real one, watching a version of herself throw a shoe.

"She'll know which parts I made up," Olivier said.

"She already knows which parts are true," Rocco said. "She was there before you were."

At the Thursday run, Olivier stood at the back again. When the narrator stepped out of the scene and said the line about not remembering it right, he heard a sound in the second row and realized his mother had come anyway, uninvited, sitting with her coat still on. She watched the whole thing without moving. At the end she didn't come to the stage, and she didn't cry, and when Olivier finally made his way over through the folding chairs she was holding the program with the shoe scene creased into a small square between her fingers.

"The door didn't click twice," she said. "It clicked once. I counted, every night after, for a year."

She held out the program so he could see the crease, a small hard square she had made without noticing. "Fix it," she said, and pushed past him toward the exit, and he stood there in the emptying room hearing, absurdly, the latch in his head, once, then once again.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The STAR method answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result.
story:
Logan's interview at the coffee shop on Miller Street was on Saturday at ten, and by Thursday evening he had rehearsed nothing except the route, which he had walked twice, timing himself from the bus stop to the door.

His mother kept asking how the preparation was going, in the tone of someone asking about a dentist appointment, and finally he admitted that he hadn't prepared at all. She produced a folded printout from some website called Interview Tips for Teens and left it on the kitchen table beside his cereal bowl, which was her way of pontificating without saying a word.

The printout was mostly useless, full of advice like "be yourself" and "dress one level above the job," but near the bottom there was a paragraph about a thing called the STAR method. Logan read it twice. It said that the STAR method answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result. He read it a third time because it sounded like something a guidance counselor would invent, a widget for making human beings sound organized.

He called Brynn, who had survived three interviews the previous summer and treated the whole subject with the calm of a veteran.

"So they'll ask you about a time something went wrong," Brynn said over the phone, while somewhere in the background a sibling was being obstreperous about a remote control. "Everybody asks that. It's the only question they have."

"I read about this STAR thing," Logan said. "It seems fake."

"It's not fake, it's a container. You still have to put something in it." Brynn yawned. "Tell them about the history project."

The history project was the obvious candidate and also the humiliating one. Junior year, a group of five assigned to build something about the Cold War, and Logan had ended up doing the entire presentation the night before because two members hadn't contributed and one, a boy whose name Logan had gratefully forgotten, had contributed only a slide of unattributed images he'd found somewhere. Logan had said nothing at the time. He had simply stayed up until three, rebuilt the deck, and presented it the next morning while the others stood behind him like a honor guard that had done nothing honorable. When Ms. Weiss asked afterward who had made the revisions, Logan had hesitated just long enough for the silence to answer for him, and she had given him a look he still thought about, half approval and half something more complicated, a kind of disappointment aimed in a direction he couldn't name.

The problem, he explained to Brynn, was that the story made him sound either like a saint or like a doormat, and he didn't want to be either.

"Then don't tell it that way," Brynn said. "Tell the part where you decided to say something. Because you did decide, right?"

He had decided. He had drafted a message to the group chat saying that next time the work needed to be divided in writing at the start, and then he had deleted it, and then two days later he had sent a shorter version, one that sounded less like rectitude and more like a person negotiating with his own fear of conflict. One member had apologized. The unattributed-images boy had responded with a thumbs-up, which Logan chose to interpret however was convenient on any given day.

"So the situation is the project," Logan said slowly, writing it out on the back of a receipt. "The task was getting it done without the group falling apart. The action is the message I sent. The result is..." He stopped. "The result is we finished, and the next project had a written division of labor because I brought it up. That's actually true."

"That's actually true," Brynn agreed, in the voice of someone handing back a burden that had never been theirs.

On Saturday he arrived nine minutes early, which he understood was itself a kind of statement. The manager was younger than he'd expected, maybe twenty-five, with a name tag he couldn't read at that distance and a clipboard she never looked at. She asked the predictable question by the espresso machine, something with the words "challenging situation" in it, and Logan heard his own voice go into the container: the situation, the task, the action, the result, delivered in that order, roughly, with one wobble when he mispronounced "unattributed." She nodded twice. Then she asked a question no method had prepared him for, which was whether he could work Sundays, and he said yes before he had checked whether it was true, and only on the walk to the bus stop did he begin to work out what he would tell his mother.

The call came Monday while he was toasting bread. She offered him the job and he accepted it, and afterward he stood in the kitchen holding the phone, and texted Brynn a single line: "STAR works. Sunday is a problem."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: A home with a 1 percent yearly flood chance has about a 26 percent chance of flooding at least once during a 30-year mortgage.
story:
Emile had signed up for Ms. Sutton's geography elective because it met last period and the room had good windows, and for the first three weeks that was all the class was to him: light on long tables, a laptop cart, the smell of whiteboard marker. Then Ms. Sutton assigned the flood project. Each student would use the school's geographic information system to layer two maps of the city, flood risk and housing, and write about whatever the overlap showed. Emile pulled his chair up to the terminal beside Claudia, who was already dragging a shaded polygon across the screen with the confidence of someone who had done this at a cousin's house.

"You're not letting it snap," she said, watching his layer slide out of alignment. "Let the software transliterate it, basically. It converts the paper map into the grid. You have to trust the grid." Emile didn't entirely trust the grid, but he let go of the polygon and watched it settle over the census blocks, the floodplain in pale blue bleeding across a neighborhood he recognized from the bus route, blocks of narrow houses with chain-link yards.

Here was what surprised him: the blue did not sit on empty land. It sat on houses, hundreds of them, a street of them, a school. He thought of Uncle Rafael, a family friend who had just bought a place near the river and had shown Emile the deck in June, pointing at the water with the pride of a man who had out-negotiated the seller. "Got it under asking," he'd said. "Bank didn't even blink." Emile had admired that, the way he admired anyone canny with money, because he was not, and knew he was not. He'd stood on the deck and thought the river looked tame.

At home that night he looked up the number Uncle Rafael's realtor had apparently quoted, one percent. One percent chance of flooding in any given year, which sounded, to Emile, like almost nothing. But something about it nagged at him, the same way a wrong answer in the margin of a math test nags before you find the arithmetic. A mortgage is thirty years, he thought. A house doesn't get one year; it gets thirty of them. He ran the compounding the way Ms. Sutton had shown them for population growth, one minus the yearly chance, raised to the thirtieth power, subtracted from one. The screen said about twenty-six percent. He sat back. He read it again. A home with a one percent yearly flood chance had about a twenty-six percent chance of flooding at least once during a thirty-year mortgage. One in four. He said it out loud to the empty kitchen, and it sounded different out loud, heavier, like a coin that had gained weight in his hand.

The next day he told Claudia at the terminal, keeping his voice low because the fact felt private somehow, borrowed. "Twenty-six percent over thirty years. That's what one percent a year actually adds up to." She stopped dragging her polygon. "That's brutal," she said. "My aunt's street is in your blue zone, did you see? Willow Bend." They both looked at the screen, where Willow Bend sat under the floodplain like a sentence under a correction. "So is Uncle Rafael's," Emile said. He had never thought of a map as something that could argue before, but this one was arguing, quietly, with a deck and a negotiation and a bank that hadn't blinked.

Chelsea, two seats over, leaned into their conversation the way she did, chin on her hand. "It's just a model," she said. "The blue part's a hundred-year thing, right? It's an aesthete's version of a swamp, all soft edges. Real floods do whatever they want." Emile considered this. She wasn't wrong that the map was smooth where the world was jagged, and he liked her for saying so; she had a way of distrusting beautiful things that he suspected was more honest than his way of trusting them. But smooth or not, the number behind the blue was arithmetic, not art. Twenty-six percent did not care about the edges.

He wrote his report over the weekend, and the hard part was not the overlays, which by now he could snap together in his sleep. The hard part was the paragraph where he tried to hold both things at once: that his uncle's house was a good deal and a sound roof and a garden going in this spring, and that the map said what it said, and that both of these could be true and neither cancelled the other. He left a sentence in about his own uncertainty, about how he couldn't tell whether the map's caution was wiser than his uncle's optimism or just colder. He thought about cutting it, because it made him look like he hadn't finished thinking. Then he left it in, and pressed print.

Monday, he called Uncle Rafael, mostly to hear his voice. "You looked up my house on a school computer?" his uncle said, laughing, but not entirely, and then, quieter, "Twenty-six, you said?" Emile confirmed the number, exactly as he'd found it, and heard the deck creak through the phone as his uncle stepped out onto it to look at the river.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A violin's four strings are tuned in perfect fifths to G, D, A and E, from lowest to highest.
story:
The auditorium smelled of dust and radiator paint, and Tyson sat on the edge of the stage with a rented violin that still had someone else's rosin dust in its seams. He had signed up for the pit orchestra because Clare had said, back in September, that they needed someone, anyone, and because he had wanted, quietly, to be needed. Two months later he could produce a sound like a door complaining, and the winter concert was nine days away.

Clare sat cross-legged beside the piano, her own violin across her lap, tuning by ear. She had been playing since she was seven, and she watched him wrestle with the instrument the way you watch someone parallel park badly: sympathetic, unable to help. "You're fighting it," she said. "Stop pressing so hard with your thumb."

"I'm not fighting it," Tyson said, and then the bow skidded and produced a note so ugly that Shaan, sprawled in the fourth row with the percussion parts he was supposed to be memorizing, called out, "That one's going on my phone."

Mr. Dang came up the aisle with his coffee, unhurried, and stopped at the lip of the stage. He had a way of standing that made you feel he had all afternoon, though the calendar said otherwise. "Play me your G string," he said. Tyson set his fingers down and drew the bow, and a sour wobble came out, not the open, woody tone Clare got from hers. He tried again, then again, and on the third attempt he realized he wasn't even on the string he thought he was. His fingers had migrated up the fingerboard without his permission, and he was hearing A where he had promised G.

"Which one is that?" Mr. Dang asked.

"The G," Tyson said, and Clare shook her head.

"That's the A." She laid her own violin flat in her lap and touched each string as she spoke. "G, D, A, E, lowest to highest. They're tuned in perfect fifths." She said it the way you'd recite a doorway you'd walked through ten thousand times, and Tyson understood that for her it wasn't information anymore, it was furniture.

Mr. Dang sipped his coffee. "When I started, I kept mixing them up for a year. My teacher gave me a sentence to remember them. Good Dogs Ate Everything." He shrugged, as if embarrassed by his own usefulness. "Stupid sentence. It stuck anyway."

Tyson felt something loosen. All fall he had been treating the fingerboard as a mystery, four identical wires and a fog, and here was a map with an idiot's rhyme on it, and it worked. He put his first finger on the D string and thought, dog, dog, dog, and the note that came out was the note he wanted, round and true, and Clare looked up from tightening her bow and said, "Oh."

They ran the first movement until six o'clock. His left shoulder ached in a new place, a muscle he had apparently been refusing to use, and the tips of his fingers had gone tender and pink, beginning the slow hardening that Clare promised would happen whether he wanted it or not. Shaan recuperated between run-throughs by lying flat across two seats with his drumsticks balanced on his chest like a fallen soldier, and once, when Tyson missed the same entrance three times, Shaan sat up and called him a petulant virtuoso, which was unfair, since Tyson was neither, but it made Clare laugh so hard she had to put her bow down.

Walking out through the lobby, Tyson understood something he could not fully explain. He had wanted to be needed, and he had also wanted, in a way he was less proud of, to be impressive, to be the boy who picked up the violin in October and played it by December, and those two wants had been tangled together all season like strings in a case. Maybe everyone who did anything was partly an egoist and partly something better, and you never got to find out which part was steering. He didn't know yet. The concert would tell him something, or it wouldn't.

At the doors, Clare caught his sleeve. "Same time tomorrow," she said. "Start on the G this time. Good dogs."

"Good dogs," he said, and pushed the door open into the cold.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Early Action in US college admissions gives an early decision but is non-binding, so an admitted student may still choose not to enroll.
story:
The envelope had been an anachronistic touch, Evan thought, actual paper in an era of portals and status checkers, and he had almost thrown it out before recognizing the crest. Now it lay open on the kitchen table between his laptop and a cold mug of tea, the word CONGRATULATIONS angled toward the window where December light was already failing at four in the afternoon. His mother kept touching the corner of it on her way to the stove, the way she touched the newspaper when something in it was about her.

"So that's it," she said. "You're in. You can stop with all the essays."

Evan turned the laptop toward her so she could see the screen, where six other applications waited in various states of incompleteness, their deadlines strung across January like a rope bridge he was only halfway along. "It's Early Action," he said. "I get the answer early, but it doesn't bind me. If I get in, I can still say no."

"You'd say no to this?"

"I might. I don't know yet."

She set down the dish towel and studied him the way she studied the radiator when it made a new sound. The acceptance was to a good school, a famous one, the kind whose name made cashiers at the grocery store raise their eyebrows. But it was far from home, and the financial aid letter wouldn't come until spring, and somewhere in the middle of all that was a question he hadn't figured out how to parametrize, to reduce to its actual variables instead of the fog of feeling around them: whether he wanted the school or wanted to be the kind of person who got into it.

Brenden texted at five. u got in?? grace says ur in. evan. EVAN. Evan typed back that yes, he was in, and no, it didn't mean anything was decided, and watched the three dots appear and disappear while Brenden composed something he clearly kept deleting. When the message came it was only: sick. want me to come over. Grace is here, we're watching your street like hawks.

They arrived with a bag of clementines and no pretense of having anything else to do. Grace dropped into the chair across from the envelope and pulled it toward her without asking, which was how Grace did most things. "You know what this means," she said. "You're done. You can burn the Common App. ritually. I'll bring the matches."

"It's non-binding," Evan said. "That's the whole point of Early Action. I get the early decision and I keep my options."

Grace's face changed, and he understood that she had been building a theory of his future on the assumption that his was settled, that hers could then be settled against it, the two of them bracketing the uncertainty together. Brenden, peeling a clementine with surgical care, said nothing, which for Brenden was speech.

"You're still applying other places," Grace said. It wasn't a question.

"Six more. And the money's not even decided yet. The aid comes later, so I won't actually know what it costs until spring."

"Then what was today?" She meant the envelope, the phone call to his father, the picture his mother had taken of him holding it, which was already on the family chat with eleven exclamation points from an aunt.

"A door opening," Evan said. "Not a door closing behind me."

Ms. Oliveira from next door knocked while Brenden was still there, holding a tin of the lemon cookies she made whenever anyone on the street had news, a sort of indemnity against celebration going unmarked, as though joy unobserved might later be reclaimed. She had taught English at the high school for thirty years and had opinions about admissions that she delivered while looking pointedly at the clementine peels. "You'll finish the others," she said, and when Evan started to explain she held up a hand. "I'm not explaining. I'm telling you what you already know, which is a different service."

Later, after everyone had gone and the table was cleared except for the envelope, Evan sat with the six unfinished applications and did the arithmetic again. Finishing them cost him his winter break, cost his mother the settled certainty she'd been carrying around the kitchen all day, cost Brenden and Grace the version of spring where everything was already known. Not finishing them cost him leverage, options, the ability to compare aid packages that didn't exist yet. He had spent a year learning that both of those things could be true, that a decision made twice was not the same decision, and he still could not say which truth outweighed the other.

He opened the essay document and read the half-written paragraph about his grandfather's workshop, the one that had seemed profound in October and now seemed like something written by a younger, more certain person. He placed his hands on the keyboard. Outside, the streetlight came on, and Ms. Oliveira's kitchen window across the way went yellow, and somewhere down the block a car door slammed once and did not slam again.

"Okay," he said to the empty kitchen, and typed his name at the top of the next application.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In a 2014 study led by David Yeager, students were more likely to revise essays when critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them.
story:
The chain-link gate still sang on its hinge when Nicolas arrived, the way it had since he was eight, and the court behind the elementary school was empty except for Mischa, who was shooting free throws in the flat light of four o'clock. Nicolas had been turning a sentence over all day, the way you turn a stone in your pocket until the edges go smooth, and the sentence was something like: your passing is fine, keep it up. He knew it was a lie. He knew it was a kind lie, the kind you give a friend, and he knew it would not help Mischa make the travel team on Saturday.

"You came," Mischa said, without looking. The ball clanked off the back rim, and he chased it into the weeds near the fence. "Coach says I pass like I'm apologizing. That was a direct quote, by the way. 'Like you're apologizing.'"

"He shouldn't have said it like that." Nicolas caught the ball when Mischa rolled it back, felt the grit of the court on his palms. What he did not say was that the coach was, in the blunt way of coaches, right. Mischa threw passes the way some people beseech: soft, hopeful, aimed vaguely at wherever a person might generously be. Twice in Tuesday's scrimmage the ball had sailed out of bounds untouched.

Erika showed up ten minutes late with her bike helmet still on and a granola bar in her teeth, because she never did anything with fewer than three things going on. She sat on the low wall by the swings and watched them run a two-man drill, Nicolas cutting to the elbow, Mischa finding him, not finding him. On the third bad pass she called out, "You're releasing it before you look. That's all it is." Then, to Nicolas, quieter, "So say the rest."

"There isn't a rest."

"There's a whole rest. You've got the face you get before a math test."

Nicolas wiped his forehead with his shirt and bought time by resetting the drill, but time did not buy anything. He understood, in the slippery way you understand things you'd rather not, that he had two loyalties in his hands and they did not fit together. One was to Mischa, who had sat with him through his father's surgeries two winters ago and asked for nothing, not even conversation. The other was to a stranger he'd never meet: the version of Mischa on Saturday who could actually make the team, who deserved to hear the truth before some coach with a whistle decided his future in eleven minutes of scrimmage. Kindness and honesty, he'd always assumed, were the same thing wearing different clothes. On the court, in the dust, they were not the same thing at all. The kind lie protected Mischa from feeling bad, and honesty, done badly, protected Nicolas from having to be careful. He wanted a third thing, and he didn't have a word for it yet.

Erika took the ball, dribbled twice, and dropped it. "My brother told me about this thing last night, actually. In 2014, this researcher David Yeager ran a study where students were more likely to revise their essays when the critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed the student could meet them." She shrugged, as if embarrassed to have been paying attention. "One sentence. That was the difference."

"One sentence," Nicolas repeated.

"One sentence. It's not a trick, it's just saying the true second thing out loud." She meant it practically, he could tell, the way she meant everything, but he heard it the way you hear a door unlock. The artifice he'd been building all day, the fine false compliment, the elaborate cushioning, had been exactly that: artifice, a scaffold around nothing. What Mischa needed wasn't a softer version of the truth or a harder one. He needed the truth plus the other truth, the one Nicolas had been carrying without saying because saying it felt gratuitous, like handing someone a gift in front of people who got nothing.

He took the ball back to the arc, spun it once, and passed it hard to Mischa, chest height, so it stung a little. "I think you can make this team," he said. "I actually think that, so listen. When you pass, you're letting go before your eyes find me. You're throwing to where I was. The fix is one count: look, then release. Look, then release." It came out faster than he'd planned, and it sat there in the air afterward, and Mischa stood holding the ball against his hip with an expression Nicolas couldn't read at all, which frightened him more than anger would have.

For a while nobody spoke. The swings ticked in the wind behind them. Then Mischa said, "Again," and passed back, and they ran it eleven more times, and on the ninth, Nicolas cut, and the ball arrived exactly where his hands were going, hard and flat, no apology in it. Mischa made a sound like a laugh getting away from him. Erika, still on the wall with the helmet finally off, said nothing, which from her was a kind of applause.

They played until the light went amber and the streetlights in the parking lot buzzed on, one of them flickering. Nicolas knew the sentence he'd said wasn't a cure, that Saturday might still end with Mischa's name absent from the list, that one good pass in an empty playground weighs nothing against eleven minutes in a gym full of evaluators. He didn't pretend otherwise, even to himself. What he knew was smaller and harder to hold: the truth had cost him something, the safe version of himself, the friend who only ever says yes, and he had paid it, and Mischa was still standing at the arc.

"One more," Mischa said, bouncing the ball once, twice. "Look, then release. Say it with me this time."

"Look, then release," Nicolas said, and cut to the elbow.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: German capitalizes every noun, not only names, which helps a reader of a German article spot the nouns in a sentence at a glance.
story:
The newspaper lay on the café table in Munich like a small square country Nicole had no map for. Her father had gone to order, her mother was photographing the fountain across the square, and Nicole had picked up the paper mostly because her phone had no signal and the silence felt too large. The headline was a fence of words, nearly all of them capitalized, and she frowned at it the way you frown at someone speaking to you in a room full of noise.

"Was ist das," she said under her breath, and then, because the words looked important, she said them again with more gravitas, and the woman at the next table glanced over and smiled before returning to her own paper.

Jose slid into the chair across from her with two pastries balanced on a napkin. "You've been staring at that for ten minutes. Is it a crossword?"

"It's the news. Look at this." She turned the paper toward him. "Why do half the words start with capitals? Not just the beginnings of sentences. There's a capitalized word in the middle of everything."

Jose leaned in, chewing. He was the most garrulous person in their traveling group, normally capable of filling a train car with commentary, but here he only squinted and said, "Maybe they're all names?"

"They can't all be names. Look." She put her finger under a sentence in the article about the river, the one her father had pointed out that morning because the trip was supposedly educational. "This word is capitalized. Then this one, then this one again later. And these other words, the little ones, stay lowercase no matter where they sit."

Leona arrived with Ms. Li, their neighbor from back home, who had invited herself along on the family trip with a breeziness no one had quite known how to refuse. Ms. Li set down her coffee and said nothing, which Nicole had learned was her way of waiting to see whether you would figure something out or fold.

Nicole read the sentence again, sounding it out. "Flut, Warnung, Wasser." She didn't know what they meant, not exactly, but the article had a photo of a flooded street, and she guessed. Flood, warning, water. All three capitalized. And the small lowercase words threaded between them like connective tissue. "Jose," she said slowly, "what if every noun has a capital? Not just names. Every single noun in the language."

"You think a whole country capitalizes its nouns?"

"Why not? It's like the language is labeling things for you. Every noun just stands up and announces itself." She went back to the beginning of the article and ran her eyes down the left edge, and the capitals made a kind of skeleton, a frame she could see before she understood a word of what hung on it. Suddenly the sentence had a shape. The capitalized words were the bones, the bones carried the meaning, and the lowercase words were the joints. She could guess which words were doing the work.

"Read it out loud," Ms. Li said. "Summarize it for us. Even badly."

Nicole's first attempt collapsed halfway. She had the skeleton and none of the flesh, and she said so, and Leona laughed, not unkindly. On the second try Nicole ignored the little words entirely and translated only the capitalized ones, touching each with her fingertip: "River. Levels. Weekend. Rain. South. Danger." Then she arranged them with her own grammar, the way she'd arrange notes for a class presentation, and said, "The river levels this weekend, because of rain in the south, there's danger of flooding." She looked up. "Something like that. The picture helps."

"The picture helps everyone," Leona said. "That's why newspapers have pictures."

But Nicole was already checking her theory against a second article, about a train strike, and it held. Zug, Bahn, Streik, all capitalized, all nouns, standing in their sentences like small stone monuments. The exceptions she hunted for, the trap she expected, never appeared. Even ordinary words, table words, coffee words, got the treatment. She wondered whether German writers felt their nouns the way she suddenly did, as things with weight, things worth marking.

"Could presage something," Jose said, gesturing at the flood article. "Danger of flooding, sounds like it presages a bad weekend for somebody."

"It presages a bad weekend for whoever lives near that river," Nicole said. "That's my summary. Final answer." She folded the paper and put it on the corner of the table, and it sat there with a new solidity, no longer a fence but a document, something she could open again and argue with.

Ms. Li paid for the pastries and stood, collecting her scarf. "Tomorrow's paper," she said, "you read the whole front page."

"That's a threat," Nicole said, and Ms. Li almost smiled.

Her parents came back with a map, asking about the afternoon, the museum or the river walk, and Nicole looked past them toward the fountain, thinking that the river in the article was a real river, somewhere north, rising or not rising under real rain, while here the light lay flat and golden on the cobblestones and nothing at all was flooded.

"River walk," she said. "I want to see whether the water's high."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: In his Poetics, Aristotle said a well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end.
story:
Anna had pushed the coffee table against the wall and set up a row of folding chairs in her living room, which made the room look, her mother said, like a very small and unsuccessful airport. The chairs were for the reading. In two weeks Mr. Vargas's drama elective would perform ten-minute plays drawn from the students' own lives, and Anna had written hers in three nights, mostly on her phone, mostly after midnight.

Aidan arrived first, carrying a bag of chips he intended to share with no one. He had wanted to act in the play, any part, and had been quietly wounded when Anna cast him as the little brother, a role with four lines, two of which were "I'm telling Mom." Jon came next, holding the script like it might leak. Jon was directing his own play at school, about two roommates arguing over a broken lease, and had come to Anna's partly out of friendship and partly, Anna suspected, to scout the competition.

"Okay," Anna said. "Places. I'll read my mom, you're my brother, Jon does everything else."

They read it. The play was about the afternoon in seventh grade when Anna's mother forgot to pick her up from swim practice, and she waited on the curb for two hours, and when the car finally came neither of them said anything the whole way home. On the page it had seemed complete. Out loud, it stopped. The last line was the car door closing, and then Aidan looked up from his chips and said, "That's it?"

"That's it," Anna said.

"Nothing changed, though. She's still mad, the mom's still whatever, and I eat a chip." He held up the chip as evidence.

Jon leaned forward, and Anna could see the scout in him, the autodidact who had spent one weekend reading everything ever written about playwriting and now considered himself dangerous. "It's like the thing," he said. "Aristotle, whatever. A well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end. You've got a beginning and a middle."

"A whole," Aidan repeated, with his mouth full. "You've got two-thirds of a whole. That's a fraction."

"It has to be a whole," Jon said again, mildly, because he had made his point and knew it.

Anna sat on the arm of the couch and felt peevish, at Aidan for the chips, at Jon for being right, at seventh-grade Anna for not saying anything in the car so that there would be something to write an ending about. The trouble was that the real afternoon had ended the way real afternoons end, with nothing resolved and a door closing. She had wanted the play to be true. But true, apparently, was not the same as finished, and she could not figure out whether that was a problem with the afternoon or a problem with Aristotle.

"Can I try something?" she said. She took the script back from Jon, flipped to the last page, and wrote for a minute while Aidan read the nutrition facts aloud in a dramatic voice. "New ending. The car stops at a red light. My mom says, 'There was an accident on Route Nine, I called the school.' And my character says, 'I know. They told me.' And they still don't say anything else. But she reaches over and locks my door, the old way, the way she did when I was little."

"Locks the door," Jon said slowly.

"It's not forgiveness," Anna said. "It's not even an apology. But something shifts, and you can see it, and the light turns green."

Aidan set down the chips, which for him was a standing ovation, and did the little brother's line, "I'm telling Mom," with what he clearly felt was nuance. Then he wanted to know if the little brother could have a fifth line, possibly a joke, possibly about the accident being fake, and Anna said absolutely not, and he negotiated her up to a stage direction in which he waves from the window.

They ran it twice more. The second time through, Anna played her own younger self and found it stranger than she expected, saying her own old silence out loud, watching Jon sit in for her mother with a folded posture that was almost right and not at all. It was like hearing a recording of your voice, except the voice was you standing on a curb at twelve years old with wet hair. Aidan asked whether she ever found out what her mom had actually been doing that day, and Anna said she never asked, and the room got quiet in the way it does when a fact like that lands.

When they left, she stood among the folding chairs in the empty living room, script in hand, and read the new ending once more, alone. There was still a green light in it, and after the light, nothing written. She picked up her phone, found her mother's name, and started typing, then deleted it, then typed a shorter thing: question about the play, call me when you're home. She set the phone face up on the pushed-away coffee table, where she could see it, and began stacking the chairs.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In her 2017 book 'Radical Candor', Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly.
story:
The bell for free swim rang at four, which meant Cohen had exactly two days to fix what nobody wanted to name. His canoe partner, Shelby, kept dropping her paddle blade too early on the left side, and every time she did, the boat yawed wide around the buoy and they lost a second, sometimes two. The camp regatta was Saturday morning. Adrien, who steered the other tandem boat, had watched all of it from the dock and said nothing, and when Cohen pressed him that evening, Adrien only shrugged and said Shelby seemed happy lately, happier than she'd been all session, and why ruin that.

Cohen understood the impulse. Shelby's parents were divorcing, everyone knew it, and she had cried once in the boathouse in June, quietly, into a towel, until Ms. Ahmadi sat down beside her without saying anything at all. Being kind to her felt like the obvious rule. But being kind and saying nothing were not the same thing, and the difference kept snagging on him like a splinter he couldn't find.

At the crepuscular edge of Thursday, when the lake went silver and the counselors called the last boats in, Cohen stayed behind on the dock with the dog-eared paperback Ms. Ahmadi had left on the picnic table, the one she'd been reading all month. It was called Radical Candor, by Kim Scott, and on the inside cover Ms. Ahmadi had penciled a single line: good feedback means caring personally and challenging directly, both at once. Cohen read it twice. He thought of his father, who challenged everyone directly and cared about nobody's feelings, and of Adrien, who cared about everyone's feelings and challenged nobody at all. It occurred to him that the two men in his life were each half of something, and that the halves had never been in the same room.

Friday morning he found Adrien hauling a canoe up the ramp. "You saw her stroke," Cohen said. "At the turn buoy. You saw it twenty times."

Adrien shifted the boat onto his shoulder. "I'm not the coach."

"You're her friend. That's supposed to count for more, not less." Adrien started to equivocate, something about not being Shelby's keeper and not wanting to embarrass her in front of the younger campers, and Cohen let him run out of words, because the words were all fence and no gate. Then he said, "If we lose tomorrow because nobody told her, that's on us. Not on her."

Shelby was at the picnic tables doing lanyard string, of all things, tongue between her teeth. Cohen sat down across from her and his heart did something awkward. "Can I tell you something about your left stroke? It's small. It's one thing."

She looked up, wary, and he remembered the towel, and Ms. Ahmadi sitting wordless, and he made sure the first thing out of his mouth was true and not strategy. "Your timing on the pull is the best on this lake. I'm not saying that to soften anything. It's just true. The blade comes out too early on the left, and the boat swings wide at the buoy. Two seconds. If you hold it a half beat longer, we get those seconds back."

Shelby set the lanyard down. "Adrien never said anything."

"Adrien thinks being nice means not telling you stuff. I think he's wrong, and I'm going to tell him so." She laughed, a short surprised sound, and then she said, "Show me the half beat," and they walked down to the water and took out a canoe without asking, which felt like its own small crime and was worth it. He counted the stroke aloud, one and two and hold, and she held it, and the boat tracked straight through the turn for the first time all week, and she yelled so loudly that a heron lifted off the far bank.

Later, at the campfire, it felt like pure synchronicity that Ms. Ahmadi dropped onto the log beside him just as he was planning what to say to Adrien. "I see someone found my book," she said, nodding at his back pocket, where the cover was sticking out like a white flag. "That author, Kim Scott, she'd say you did the caring part and the challenge part at the same time. Rare, at sixteen." Cohen admitted he hadn't finished it, hadn't even gotten past the inside cover and the first chapter, and that he still wasn't sure whether he'd been honest with Shelby because it was right or because he wanted to win. Ms. Ahmadi said the two motives could ride in the same boat without capsizing it, and then she stole his marshmallow, which seemed like her own version of both at once.

Saturday came gray and warm. Cohen and Shelby lined up at the start with six other boats, and Adrien, who had finally heard the whole story and had gone quiet for an hour before finding Shelby to say, "You already know I should've said it sooner, so I'm saying it," sat in his own boat two lanes over. The starter raised the flag. Shelby's blade went in clean, held the half beat, came out at the exact moment Cohen's did, and the boat leapt forward like something released rather than pushed. Around the first buoy, no yaw, no wide swing, just water shearing off the hull in two flat sheets.

They took the turn side by side with Adrien's boat, close enough that Cohen could hear him counting the stroke aloud for his own partner, one and two and hold, and he laughed into the wind of it, and put his head down, and pulled.
